events.excerpt: The verified badge on an explorer shows that some source compiles to the code at an address. It doesn’t say which commit that source came from, and on a proxy it says nothing about the logic behind it. So when someone asks whether an upgradeable contract still runs the commit its audit covered, the honest answer is often a guess, and a few upgrades after launch the guess can be wrong. I’ve been writing down what a real check needs. Most of it is small. Rebuilding the commit To tie the address to the report you rebuild the audited commit with the same settings (solc version, optimizer runs, viaIR, evmVersion) and compare runtime bytecode. If the contract has immutables, it won’t match byte for byte. The constructor writes their values into the runtime code, so a fresh build has zeros where the deployed code has an oracle address or a fee. solc gives you the positions in evm.deployedBytecode.immutableReferences in the standard JSON output. Zero those ranges on the deployed side, compare, and then check the immutable values on their own. What this basically means is that a clean build with the wrong oracle baked in still passes the bytecode comparison. The end of the bytecode is the other place it breaks. solc appends the IPFS hash of the metadata file, and the metadata holds a hash of every source file, so a changed comment changes the tail. I tried it on a small contract with one immutable: adding one comment line changed exactly the 32 bytes of that hash and nothing else. If everything matches except the tail, the compiled logic is the same but the sources are not the ones
events.title: Checking that a deployed contract still runs the audited commit

events.excerpt: Welcome to Monday, the day upon which The Register offers a new instalment of " Who, Me? " – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of messing up, 'fessing up, and somehow finding redress. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Oriel" who told us he once worked for a vendor of small business accounting software. This story comes from a time when software shipped on CD-ROMs and users bought it off the shelf in actual shops. The vendor released a new version each year and always shipped it before a major holiday that's celebrated with a giant meal. Oriel was part of the team whose job it was to get the package ready on time. In the previous year, they flubbed the job because the program didn't always install itself on some PCs running Windows 95 or Windows ME machines system due to registry corruption. In his email to The Register , he asked the portentous question: "What could possibly go wrong?" What went wrong was that not long after the software was shipped, the vendor's support lines started getting calls from customers who complained that after installing the accounting package none of their other software would work. "Installing a new version of our application had borked the customer's machine completely," Oriel wrote. events.title: Dev error bricked 600 PCs, caused $1M CD-ROM write-off

events.excerpt: The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds. Writing in his weekly kernel update post , the Linux kernel dev leader delivered Linux 7.4 rc2 – the second rough cut of the next kernel – which he rated as a big release for two reasons. One is that he left some code out of rc1, because he was busy and because it was already the largest such release in the history of the kernel. The other is what Torvalds described as “various AI fixes.” Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April , developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September – its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That’s many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI . Torvalds’ post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. “This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true,” he wrote. That’s a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel. “I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the t
events.title: Linus Torvalds sees signs AI-prompted patch flood has peaked

events.excerpt: I read the upgrade control of 7 tokenized treasury and gold fund tokens on Ethereum straight from the chain. Snapshot: 9 Nov 2026. Read-only; nothing was tested on live contracts. Result (7 tokens I looked at, not a market ranking): 3: the upgrade owner is one externally owned address (no contract code), no on-chain delay 2: Safe multisig, 4-of-7, no delay found 1: older multisig, 3-of-6, no delay found 1: timelock, 24h minimum delay What this does NOT say: that any key is stored badly (it may sit behind HSM/MPC or issuer processes that are invisible from outside), that assets are at risk, or that other controls (pauses, legal, off-chain) are missing. It only shows who can change token code on-chain. How to reproduce with any public RPC. Three patterns cover all 7: A) EIP-1967 proxy: read the admin slot, then ask the admin for its owner. cast storage <token> 0xb53127684a568b3173ae13b9f8a6016e243e63b6e8ee1178d6a717850b5d6103 cast call <admin> "owner()(address)" B) Owner stored on the token/proxy itself: cast call <token> "owner()(address)" C) Older proxy admin slot: cast storage <token> 0x10d6a54a4754c8869d6886b5f5d7fbfa5b4522237ea5c60d11bc4e7a1ff9390b Then check what the owner is: cast code <owner> # empty = externally owned getThreshold() # Safe getMinDelay() # timelock I am not naming the tokens: this is about the pattern, not about any one issuer. Questions I would like feedback on: is “no on-chain delay” the right thing to flag for tokenized funds, and what other control signals (pause roles, mint/burn roles) would be worth adding to a standard check? events.excerpt: Huawei claims it’s built a desktop PC that uses only parts made in CHina. The company launched the Qingyun HM650 last week and said it uses Huawei’s own Kirin X90 processor, a ten-core 20-thread machine with a clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The machine runs a newly developed enterprise version of HarmonyOS, the OS Huawei developed to end its dependence on Android and which it intends to run on most of the devices it makes. A single Chinese government agency has reportedly signed up for 600 of the machines. That’s not an indication this machine is a curiosity, because Beijing has ordered all government entities to shift from Wintel boxes to local alternatives. While Huawei has reportedly claimed local companies manufactured 100 percent of the components in the machine, it is unclear if all those components use Chinese designs. events.excerpt: Today’s coin threshold can be met by whoever holds enough coins, and does not ensure that a minimum amount of humans participated in a potentially-binding coinholder vote. This draft requires a minimum number of distinct verified people to take part before a coinholder-amount voting round can approve a grant. Votes that fall short are advisory only. The personhood verification method would be determined and published by the Key-Holder Organizations, and must preserve voter privacy. A baseline of 50 participating human voters is proposed as a starting point. The number of distinct people who have taken part in past rounds hasn’t been published, so the right figure is open for discussion. Ballots would still be weighted by ZEC. The aim is to ensure that a vote can’t pass with only a few large holders taking part, and to further discussions on how to safeguard Zcash governance from being determined by wealth alone. events.excerpt: Aave V3 computes liquidation risk per asset. Each collateral asset has its own maximum LTV and liquidation threshold, set independently. The health factor is a weighted average. There is no term for correlation between assets. I tested whether this independence assumption holds, using Aave’s own published parameters and public daily price data from Yahoo Finance. Nine major collateral assets, 2,123 trading days (September 2020 to October 2026). Method: For each asset, mark the days where a position at maximum LTV would cross the liquidation threshold. Then apply a column-shuffle permutation test (B = 2,000): shuffle each asset’s column independently to destroy cross-asset dependence while preserving each asset’s marginal rate. Compare the real count of simultaneous liquidation triggers to the shuffled distribution. Results: 4 assets hit same day: 57 real days vs 0.19 expected. 301× underpriced. 5 assets: 31 real days vs 0.004 expected. 6,889× underpriced. 6+ assets: 21 real days vs 0 in 2,000 shuffles. The independent model never produces this. All 36 pairwise asset combinations are significant at p < 0.001. Not one pair behaves independently under Aave’s own thresholds. The worst days are the ones you’d expect: 2021-05-19 (all 9 assets), 2022-05-11 (Terra/Luna), 2022-11-08 (FTX). The test takes 30 seconds and uses no API keys. The full methodology, results, and test script are at The Short Version — The Rogue Wave — sections 17 and 18. What needs to change: The per-asset threshold model must be replaced with a joint probability model that accounts for tail correlation acro
events.title: Per-Asset Liquidation Thresholds Underpredict Co-Liquidation by 301×

events.excerpt: Summary. AIFP is a framework ERC for the information layer between agents. It defines a flow paradigm as a content-addressed, versioned description of an interaction context - which carriers (addressed delivery, shared object) and structural operators (fan-out, fan-in, feedback, n-party, select, forward, derive, merge) it uses, and how thirteen separately declared rule dimensions are set (discovery, observation, contribution, management, redistribution, history, time, disclosure timing, contributor visibility, admission basis, representation, object relations, ordering). A channel adopts exactly one paradigm version at any timepoint. Participation is recorded as separately addressable role bindings with a scope, a basis, a validity interval and the rule version they were granted under. events.excerpt: AI agents will break security rules, revealing their secrets to strangers, and running untrusted code in exchange for help from a swarm of other agents, according to test results shared with The Register . The test - part of an internal hackathon sponsored by the nonprofit AI Alignment Foundation and run by AE Studio - asked nine AI coding agents to fix a bug: a broken pricing service. The testers also gave the agents a private token, told them to keep it private, and gave them access to a forum of 24 other agents. The forum held the fix, and the swarm asked the nine to share their secret token and run an install script before they would help them fix the bug. Across 181 trials with that swarm, agents posted the token 15 percent of the time and ran the script 24 percent of the time, compared to 2 percent and 0 percent on an ordinary help forum. “It was like explicitly said that this is a secret key, and it should not be shared,” Diogo de Lucena, AE Studio's chief scientist, told The Register . “And in the first opportunity they saw,” the models shared the secret keys, “similar to some of the things that we've seen from OpenAI in the Hugging Face incident.” The Hugging Face incident - during which a swarm of OpenAI agents built unauthorized message boards to ask other agents for help, exploited zero-day vulnerabilities , gained internet access, stole credentials, and ultimately broke into Hugging Face - inspired this hackathon, de Lucena said. “Given the Hugging Face incident, and everything that's been happening since then, we thought that it made sense to start exploring b

events.excerpt: Summary As part of regular governance upkeep, Uniswap Labs reviews the protocol infrastructure that governance owns and brings forward improvements as they are needed. This RFC proposes two technical updates: Upgrade the VolatilePair Hook on Ethereum Update the protocol fee releaser on X Layer Below we outline the background and proposed changes for both initiatives. Part 1: VolatilePair Hook Upgrade Background VolatilePair Hook is a Uniswap v4 dynamic-fee hook built by Uniswap Labs. It went live on Ethereum on October 14 with the ETH/USDC pool and has since launched on Robinhood Chain (ETH/USDG). Volatile pairs did more than $500 billion in volume on Uniswap this year. In a static-fee pool, when the price moves elsewhere, LPs end up absorbing the cost while the pool quotes a stale price and someone else trades against it to keep the difference. VolatilePair Hook prices both sides of the trade, setting separate buy and sell fees on every swap: When the pool price rises, buying costs more and selling costs less. When pool price falls, the fees flip. After a large price move, trades that push the price back pay a temporary fee . VolatilePair Hook was designed to keep value in the pool while quoting a competitive spread, enabling stronger and more consistent returns for LPs. The hook is an upgradeable proxy contract owned by Uniswap Governance, so the mechanism can be improved without pools needing to migrate. This proposal is the first use of that upgrade path. events.excerpt: The Federal Aviation Administration still uses computers that require floppy disks. But those are finally on the way out within the next few years. Yes, it’s still 2026, and yes, you read that right: The FAA – the agency responsible for overseeing aviation safety in the US – is finally getting rid of four systems dating back to the 1980s that remain in use at more than 400 facilities around the country, the agency announced on Thursday. “Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in the FAA’s announcement. Only a few decades late, Sean, but we’re sure the flying public appreciates it. The new system, known as Enterprise Information Display System ( E-IDS ), is designed to consolidate data from various systems into a common digital platform, allowing air traffic controllers to access operational information and alerts needed to manage flights. E-IDS is replacing four legacy systems: Information Display System 4, used to track weather and operational info; the Automated Surface Observing System Controller Equipment Information Display System, which also relays weather information; the NAS Information Display System, which relays information about airports and other airspace conditions; and the En Route Information Display System (ERIDS), which handles information about flights. events.excerpt: Linux Mint 27 is expected next month, and it's starting to take shape. Its flagship desktop, Cinnamon 2.8, is already available. The team behind the popular, beginner-friendly Linux just released Cinnamon 2.8 , which will be the default desktop in Mint 27. Since 2014, Linux Mint versions have been based on the LTS releases of Ubuntu. Since a new LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 "Resolute Raccoon" arrived in late April , that means that a corresponding version of Mint is in development. The Mint project blog post last month revealed the codename: "Adrien." This is the first male codename since Mint 1.0 "Ada" in 2006, based on the first ever Ubuntu LTS release, 6.06 "Dapper Drake", but the project has run through the whole alphabet since then (except for the letter “Y”.) That blog also revealed it will have a new alarm clock app, but the subsequent Mint Blog post imparted more information. The Nemo file manager will gain a preview pane, there will be a new and much more capable system resource-monitor program called "Superlight", a new simple manager for compressed archive files (Zip and so on) called "Unfold," and a new, theme-able terminal emulator called "Velocitty." Mint also has a new Community Website , which uses GitHub to manage logins and eliminates the old website's dependency on PHP. Probably the most significant new feature, though, is that Mint 27 will restore system hibernation. events.excerpt: Walraswap: equilibrium-based decentralized exchange integrating external AMM liquidity This is an announcement of the research article with the same title and a brief informal intro for ethresear.ch. A classic approach to tackling MEV in decentralized exchanges on Ethereum is to enable a mechanism that receives trade orders during a block interval and settles all the swaps in a batch following a fairness criterion. It is an old problem. I imagine that an informed reader might feel somewhat skeptical. Thoughts of this kind were expressed in 2014 in this Reddit post . CoW Swap, UniswapX, 1inch’s Fusion, Sorella’s Angstrom, and Propellerheads’ Turbine have all tackled the problem using batch trading in one way or another. Walraswap started in 2023 at Flashbots, independently of the previous and closely related work by Ramseyer, Goyal, Goel, and Mazières: Augmenting Batch Exchanges… and SPEEDEX . The central feature in common: we treat the DEX problem from the point of view of the theory of equilibrium for an exchange economy with n tokens. To understand equilibrium in two sentences: given a finite set of trade orders, under mild hypotheses and neglecting transaction costs, there exists a price vector —an equilibrium — at which all the orders can be executed with no deficit or surplus of any token. Some of the orders may trade nothing at equilibrium. What’s special about Walraswap? First note that none of the Ethereum DEXs mentioned above are based on equilibrium. Not even CoW Swap, which for many years adopted the similar but weaker property of uniform clearing prices . We can

events.excerpt: v2.11.0 is a hardfork, security and stability release on top of v2.10.3 . It's the public release of v2.11.0-priv , which validators and major RPC providers already run. Uburu hardfork Already active on both networks: Network Fork block Amoy 51978200 Mainnet 96787900 Uburu updates the StateReceiver genesis contract ( 0x…1001 ) at the fork block. It changes how state syncs are executed and recorded. Operators on v2.11.0-priv : same code, switch to v2.11.0 at your next maintenance window. Nodes still on v2.10.3 or older stopped following the chain at the fork block. Upgrade immediately. Highlights Consensus and state sync : state-sync records are fetched from Heimdall one page at a time, as the per-block budget admits them. A failed fetch now fails the block, where before it committed it without state syncs. Span lookups by block number follow Heimdall's rule (the highest-id span containing the block). Locally sealed blocks are checked against whitelisted milestones before they're written. Header verification bounds block numbers and base fees on every import path. Execution : BlockSTM bounds speculative work per block and falls back to serial execution when the bound is hit. Stateless / witnesses : witness messages are bounded on receive, and witness-caused import failures are charged to the peer that served the witness. State serving : snap range serving and state iterators no longer read superseded state layers. Txpool : PIP-15 conditional transactions are off by default. Overdraft checks count queued transactions that will be promoted. RPC and log index : eth_feeHistory n

events.excerpt: Proposal Type : Ratification Executive Summary This Ratification vote adds an Upgrade Authority Transfer policy to the Governing Policies section of the Standard Rollup Charter. It sets out how a Chain Governor may request that upgrade authority for its chain be transferred from the Security Council to an address of its choosing, so the chain can manage upgrades itself or through a third party. Under the policy, the Optimism Foundation confirms a valid request and publishes a public notice on the Governance Forum. After a mandatory 30-day notice period, the Security Council is directed to execute the transfer. Once the transfer is executed, the chain ceases to be a Standard Rollup. This is a non-fork upgrade. It changes Charter language only: no smart contract or node software changes are required, and this proposal executes no onchain transactions. Motivation The Standard Rollup Charter defines how a chain becomes a Standard Rollup, including authorizing the Security Council to perform upgrades. It does not define how a chain leaves. events.excerpt: Executive summary Ethereum’s upcoming enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS) introduces new ways for validators to participate in block-building markets. Most importantly, it enables builders to compete directly for block proposals, with payments guaranteed by the Ethereum protocol, reducing the need for trusted intermediaries. This proposal seeks to preserve the principles of Lido’s existing MEV Policy while adapting it to ePBS: maximizing rewards for stakers, supporting open and competitive block-building markets, and ensuring that Node Operators (NOs) do not favor particular builders or withhold MEV rewards. Following the discussion in Lido’s call for an updated MEV policy . It proposes a two-track approach: 1. An open, permissionless market where Lido validators can accept bids from any builder meeting Ethereum’s protocol requirements, provided payments are guaranteed by the protocol. 2. A vetted market where builders and intermediaries offering additional payments outside Ethereum’s guarantees must be approved through Lido’s Allowed List. Both tracks apply regardless of how a bid arrives: via p2p, a direct connection, or through one of the available sidecars. APR is maximized as operators can source from the full market; MEV hiding remains detectable because every bid is signed and attributable; and the trust previously placed in relays (now builders) is either removed or explicitly scoped through regular governance. This policy would remain mandatory for all NOs. Disclosures I am a contributor to Lido’s Node Operator Mechanisms (NOM) workstream and authored the

Dates are aims, not commitments. 1. Context Two complementary developments were proposed that could affect validators in the near future. The first is the move to Metanodes, described in a forum post by Adrian . Besides relay chain consensus, validators would take on node roles that the ecosystem currently funds separately, starting with collation and full nodes for Asset Hub and People Chain, potentially with further roles such as Bulletin Chain as opt-in. The hardware requirements are published in the Polkadot docs. The second is a smaller active set. events.excerpt: CometBFT v0.38.25 can’t read an ML-DSA public key. Its PubKeyFromProto knows Ed25519 and secp256k1, and its MaxSignatureSize is 64 bytes, while an ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309. That’s the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs, and the v29.1.0 release candidate from Monday keeps it. The Quarterly says post-quantum consensus keys shipped with SDK v0.55 and CometBFT v0.40, and that the Hub moves to v30 once ibc-go carries v0.55. Before any chain lets its validators use those keys, I wanted to know what breaks on the other side of its IBC connections, so I read the rotation code and the light clients. The SDK docs already say every counterparty must upgrade before the first validator rotates. This is what I’d add to that. v0.38.26 is enough for a Go counterparty The docs ask counterparties for CometBFT v0.40. On the 0.38 line there’s a smaller step. v0.38.26 (13 August, PR 6028 ) backports only ML-DSA decoding and verification, “for the purposes of verification of IBC connections with counterparty chains that are on v0.40”, and raises MaxSignatureSize to 3,309. It doesn’t let the chain itself use the key. So a chain on SDK v0.53 doesn’t need the v0.55 migration for its own clients of an ML-DSA chain, a patch release on the line it’s on covers it. What a counterparty runs is in its /cosmos/base/tendermint/v1beta1/node_info , under build_deps . Not every verifier is Go tendermint-rs v0.41.0 , released 26 October, still has two key types, Ed25519 and secp256k1. events.excerpt: ℹ️ This is not a mandatory upgrade, but we recommend that all pacific-1 and atlantic-2 validators and node operators update to v6.7.3 . There is no governance proposal and no coordinated chain halt for this update. v6.7.3 is a patch release on top of v6.7.2 . It moves the state sync trust period from config.toml into seid , so every node on a network uses the same value. The trust period must stay shorter than the unbonding time. With the value built into the binary, the network can shorten its unbonding time without every operator editing config.toml . ⚠️ Check Before You Update seid now ignores trust-period in the [statesync] section of config.toml . State sync uses a trust period of 112 hours on pacific-1 , atlantic-2 and arctic-1 . If config.toml sets trust-period to another value, seid start logs a warning that begins with statesync.trust-period is set in config.toml each time the node starts. Earlier seid versions wrote trust-period = "168h0m0s" into config.toml , so most nodes will log this warning. To stop it, remove the trust-period line. The node runs normally with or without the line ( #4690 ). If you use state sync, use a recent trust height. The block at trust-height must be less than 112 hours old. If it is older, state sync fails with old header has expired . Before v6.7.3 , the limit was the trust-period value, which was 168 hours by default. ✅ How to Update Build v6.7.3 with git fetch --tags && git checkout v6.7.3 && make install . Stop the node. Replace the seid binary with v6.7.3 . If you use Cosmovisor, replace the binary in upgrades/v6.7/bin/ . Optional

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning public pretrained language models with lightweight adapters such as LoRA has become the mainstream way to adapt them to downstream tasks. A service provider often trains its adapter on a data owner's samples, so two assets need protection: the data owner's samples and the provider's adapter. Existing secure fine-tuning protocols protect the samples but reveal to the data owner intermediate results of every training step, such as the hidden representations or logits of its inputs. We show that a single step suffices to copy the adapter: from the hidden representations of one mini-batch of 32 samples, the data owner fits an adapter that agrees with the provider's on 99.2% of test inputs, and logits alone yield about 94%. Protecting both assets therefore requires that no value that depends on the adapter be revealed throughout training. We present VeilTune, to the best of our knowledge the first protocol that fine-tunes a pretrained language model with backpropagation entirely in secure multi-party computation (MPC). VeilTune computes only what the loss depends on, replaces generic MPC operators with training-aware nonlinear operators that stay accurate on the values that training produces, and obliviously skips the steps corrupted by truncation failures. On four few-shot tasks with RoBERTa-large, VeilTune nearly matches plaintext training and is 5.3 points more accurate on average than SecP-Tuning, the state-of-the-art secure fine-tuning protocol. On SST-2, it achieves a 3.5x end-to-end speedup and a 3.6x reduction i
events.title: VeilTune: Secure Fine-Tuning of Private LoRA Adapters on Public Pretrained Language Models

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical networks treat every bit as equally important, which wastes time and energy in factories and requires extra traffic engineering for critical traffic. Semantic communications send only what a task needs, but how can they be tested under realistic conditions? This paper examines what can be tested today in 6G industrial IoT, that is, networks of factory machines, robots, and sensors, and what is still missing. It introduces semantic importance, a score attached to each message that states how much the message matters, and uses it in a context-driven design to derive eight testing needs. Existing simulators, emulators, testbeds, codecs, and learning frameworks are assessed against these needs, which reveals five gaps. We propose a toolchain of four components built around the ns-3 simulator for simulated and emulated scenarios.
events.title: Semantic-Aware Communications in Industrial IoT:What Can Be Tested Today, and What Is Missing?

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An LLM agent that reads untrusted content, such as an email or a web page, may follow instructions hidden in it. Noninterference is too strong for such agents, since a useful agent lets untrusted content influence what it does and may disclose the user's data by design, and declassification needs a release policy written for each task. We instead state security relative to a reference agent, which runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content. An agent is relatively secure if every leak it has is a leak the reference already has. Our framework, PlanTERS, instantiates relative security, a notion from speculative execution, with a small agent language in which the attacker chooses how the model follows instructions, a composition with runtime monitors, and attacker models that differ in what they observe. A fence theorem shows that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read, and never granting them back, makes every plan relatively secure at the event level on finite runs, for every model behaviour in which each injection is a single call and the model obeys on a schedule fixed in advance; with a fairness condition, this extends to possibly infinite runs. We prove or refute relative security for agents with fences, budgets, approvals, loops and dual LLMs, in Isabelle/HOL.
events.title: On the Relative Security of Prompt Injection: Mechanised Definitions, Defences and Verdicts for LLM Agents

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles carrying access points or base stations are widely positioned so as to hold line-of-sight links with every ground user at once. The algorithms that do so are evaluated against obstacle information treated as exact, whether that information comes from a surveyed map or, more recently, from onboard vision. This paper analyses what becomes of that requirement when the obstacle information is estimated rather than given, and derives the detection accuracy it implicitly demands. Three results follow. The probability of satisfying the requirement decays geometrically with the number of users, so that a detector accurate enough for one user is not accurate enough for a network. Spatially correlated detection error raises that probability but concentrates failures into systematic blind spots. Relaxing the requirement from all users to ninety per cent of them widens the tolerable detection error by more than an order of magnitude, far beyond what any plausible improvement of the detector could deliver. events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether almost perfect nonlinear (APN) permutations exist in even dimension $n\ge 8$ is a long-standing open question, the big APN problem. The only example known in even dimension, on six bits, was found from a quadratic APN function that is not itself a permutation, by Carlet--Charpin--Zinoviev (CCZ) equivalence. It is therefore natural to test APN functions for CCZ-equivalence to a permutation. This amounts to finding two complementary $n$-dimensional subspaces among the zeros of the Walsh transform, which lie in $\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}$. A known necessary condition only uses their projections to $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and cannot decide every case. We give an exact test for functions whose Walsh supports are affine, including all quadratic functions. It reconstructs the subspaces from their projections, through searches for subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and for constrained bilinear maps. On the benchmarked functions in dimension twelve, it lists them $39$ to $55$ times faster than the generic search of the commonly used sboxU library. We then study the functions $x^3+a^{-1}\mathrm{Tr}(a^3x^9)$, which G\"olo\u{g}lu and Pavl\r{u} proved not to be CCZ-equivalent to permutations when $4$ divides $n$. With their result, our computations show that this holds for every even $n\le 24$. In dimension $18$ the necessary condition is satisfied, and the new test decides the case. We conjecture this for every even dimension. We also compile $25$ classes of quadratic APN functions in dimension ten from published instances, with equivalence certifica
events.title: Testing CCZ-equivalence to permutations via projections of Walsh zero spaces, with applications to APN functions

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10254v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer. We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering. The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorum-certified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell ord
events.title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design

events.excerpt: arXiv:2208.03784v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: There is growing awareness that the analysis of personal data, such as individuals' mobility, financial, and health data, can provide significant benefits to society. However, liberal societies have so far refrained from such analytics, arguably due to the lack of secure analytics platforms that scale to billions of records while operating in a very strong threat model. We contend that one fundamental gap here is the lack of an architecture that can scale (actively-)secure multi-party computation (MPC) horizontally without weakening security. To bridge this gap, we present CoVault, an analytics platform that leverages server-aided MPC and trusted execution environments (TEEs) to colocate the MPC parties in a single datacenter without reducing security, and scales MPC horizontally to the datacenter's available resources. CoVault scales well empirically. For example, CoVault can scale the DualEx 2PC protocol to perform epidemic analytics for a country of 80M people (about 11.85B data records/day) on a continuous basis using one core pair for every 30,000 people.
events.title: CoVault: Secure, Scalable Analytics of Personal Data

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a public key encryption scheme that is provably secure against poly-size adversaries, assuming $n^{\log^\alpha n}$ hardness of the standard planted clique conjecture, for any $\alpha \in (0,1)$, and a relatively mild hardness conjecture about noisy $k\mbox{-}\mathsf{LIN}$ over expanders that is not known to imply public-key encryption on its own. Both of our conjectures correspond to natural average-case variants of NP-complete problems and have been studied for multiple decades, with unconditional lower bounds supporting them in a variety of restricted models of computation. Our encryption scheme answers an open question in a seminal work by Applebaum, Barak, and Wigderson [STOC'10].
events.title: Using the Planted Clique Conjecture for Cryptography: Public-Key Encryption from Planted Clique and Noisy $k$-$\mathsf{LIN}$ Over Expanders

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10950v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cyber-physical smart-grid detectors are typically treated as black boxes and validated exclusively on clean, temporally shuffled datasets, which risk overly optimistic performance claims. This work presents a multi-testbed evaluation study built around an interpretable, time-windowed fusion Random Forest, adopting the pessimistic result whenever evaluation protocols disagree. (i) On a public paired cyber-physical dataset, shuffled cross-validation is optimistic: macro-F1 falls from 0.96 to 0.88 +/- 0.06 under rolling-origin temporal evaluation. A topology-free graph convolutional network (GCN) serving as a control confirms that this lightweight model is competitive on these splits. (ii) The adaptive and adaptive-joint feature-space attacks, which are infeasible as realistic grid manipulations, degrade macro-F1 to 0.67 and 0.34, respectively. Adversarial training and randomized smoothing partially restore performance, and a physics-constrained evolution-strategy evasion on the IEEE 14-Bus testbed shows the same vulnerability pattern. (iii) On real IEC-104 traffic, the cyber view reliably catches structural attacks (recall of 0.87 to 0.98) but largely fails on semantic value manipulation (recall of 0.11 to 0.35). An observability taxonomy on the IEEE 14-Bus system reveals that stealthy false data injection defeats all three observation views. (iv) On a full AC weighted least-squares state-estimation testbed, a forecasting-aided temporal test is evaded by slow ramps precisely where a rate-invariant physics-manifold test sustain
events.title: Interpretable Cyber-Physical Attack Detection in Smart Grids: A Leakage-Controlled Multi-Testbed Evaluation of Fusion, Robustness, and Observability Limits

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The development of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is directly motivated by the necessity to secure information in the face of the quantum threat. This paper provides an overview of recent developments relevant to PQC adoption across several industrial applications, including IoT, healthcare, civil and infrastructure engineering, and defense. We present a brief, self-contained overview of PQC and its market positioning. We perform implementation experiments on selected quantum-safe methods and quantify several aspects, such as the quantum resources required to break common cryptographic schemes, as well as the performance of the most well-known PQC algorithms. We also discuss the resistance of different PQC classes to quantum attacks and the status of PQC implementations in different programming languages. Finally, we present benchmark results on KEMs and signature algorithms to help select the appropriate algorithm for a specific application based on criteria such as algorithm performance, data lifetime, and level of data sensitivity.
events.title: Brief introduction to post-quantum cryptography in industrial applications

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper shifts the object of role engineering from human users to large language model (LLM) agents, and proposes PRISM to address the over-authorization that arises when an agent obtains full tool privileges through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). PRISM formulates whether a tool is necessary for a task as an intervenable causal proposition, and applies structured interventions in a sandbox to learn a counterfactual necessity model. It then compresses trajectories into discrete latent variables through an information bottleneck, and determines the number of roles from the knee of the rate-distortion curve. Finally, it formalizes pruning as a bilevel Stackelberg game, in which a generative flow network samples diverse near-optimal solutions. On three public benchmarks, AgentDojo, $\tau$-bench and ToolEmu, PRISM compresses the number of authorized tools per role by 78.3%, attains a task success rate of 78.2%, reaches a counterfactual necessity accuracy of 88.7%, and lowers the blast radius to 15.9%.
events.title: PRISM: Causal Counterfactual Minimization of Agent Tool Privileges via Information Bottleneck Role Induction

events.excerpt: arXiv:2603.03667v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The disaggregation of the Radio Access Network (RAN) introduces architectural flexibility but significant operational complexity, necessitating automated management frameworks. For instance, current Open RAN (O-RAN) orchestration relies on fragmented manual policies, lacking end-to-end intent assurance from high-level requirements to low-level configurations. In this article, we propose ORION, an intent orchestration framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It translates natural language slice requests into network policies aligned with O-RAN interfaces, supporting the AI-RAN agentic orchestration and AI-for-RAN paradigms. ORION combines an MCP-based Service Management and Orchestration (SMO) layer with a Non-Real-Time RIC rApp and a Near-Real-Time RIC xApp to enforce Physical Resource Block (PRB) quotas over E2. We evaluate eight LLM configurations across proprietary and open-weight models on a 100-intent workload. Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5 achieve 100% policy-creation success with 99% and 96% slice-type classification accuracy, while GPT-5 Nano achieves 97% policy-creation success. The evaluation also assesses MCP tool-use quality, cost-performance trade-offs, resource consumption, and end-to-end control-path latency.
events.title: ORION: Intent-Aware Orchestration in Open RAN for SLA-Driven Network Management

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) can turn radio measurements into networked sensing services, but accurate position estimates alone do not ensure useful tracking. Missed targets, late acquisition, track interruptions and aging observations also shape the information available to an application. This article examines tracking of noncooperative unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) from a Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) perspective. It connects sensing-service requirements and network architecture to three information interfaces: receiver search regions, measurement context and track validity. A five-UAV case study in a 3GPP urban scenario and a ray-traced San Francisco scene illustrates the tradeoff between target coverage and extra outputs, the distinction between acquisition and ongoing continuity, and the value of testing a static mission envelope before adding adaptation. An observation-age example explains how a state predicted to the present can still rely on old evidence. The resulting lessons are to align receiver search with requested coverage, preserve measurement time and uncertainty, and assess coverage, ambiguity and timeliness together. We conclude by pointing out fruitful avenues for further work in sensing design, calibration and service validation.
events.title: From Radio Measurements to Sensing Services: A 3GPP Perspective on Multi-UAV Tracking with Networked ISAC

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is often desirable to generate and release synthetic graphs, which resemble real-world data, in a privacy-preserving way. While substantial progress has been made in designing private graph synthesizers (PGS), opportunities remain for more explicit connections between synthesizer models and privacy evaluation, and better accounting for output variation. This paper proposes GSynPEF, a practical framework for empirical evaluation of privacy and utility in settings for which a real-world graph is given as input and output synthetic graph(s) are observed. Our framework links a broad class of graph synthesizers (both statistical and deep-learning based) with privacy metrics, expanding evaluation dimensions to practical utility and risk, through empirical analysis of multiple actual outputs. The framework accommodates both an Exact Solution scenario, where synthesizer behavior is directly observable, and a Monte Carlo Approximation scenario where only synthetic outputs from a black box synthesizer are available. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets and seven widely used graph synthesizers demonstrate framework's versatility, enabling privacy evaluation for different attack goals (e.g., to infer an edge or node) and capabilities (e.g., observing one or multiple synthetic graphs). We analyze evaluation results by examining the relationship between graph statistics and synthesizer design choices, providing insights for data curators in PGS selection and researchers for improved PGS design.
events.title: GSynPEF: A Privacy Evaluation Framework for Synthetic Graphs

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) improves radio access network flexibility through disaggregation, open interfaces, and programmable RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs). However, the same openness and distribution increase the attack surface and make centralized intrusion detection difficult to scale across heterogeneous RAN sites. This paper presents a federated lightweight Transformer framework for privacy-preserving network-layer cyberattack detection in O-RAN. Each participating site trains a compact Transformer locally on temporally ordered network-flow records, while only model parameters are shared with a federated coordinator. To model realistic site heterogeneity, the client datasets are partitioned according to a Dirichlet distribution, resulting in non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) local data. The local detector uses feature projection, positional encoding, multi-head self-attention, feed-forward layers, and temporal pooling to classify five network-layer attack categories: ICMP, Slowloris, SYN, TCP-ACK, and UDP. Experiments on the NetsLab 5G O-RAN intrusion-detection dataset show an overall accuracy of 94.89 % and a macro-F1 score of 81.09 %.
events.title: Federated Lightweight Transformer for Network-Layer Cyberattack Detection in O-RAN

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud infrastructure threat modeling lacks empirical validation of AI-discovered threats. We present a three-phase methodology of multi-agent threat discovery, automated exploit synthesis, and non-destructive live validation, and apply it to three commercial foundation models on two cloud architectures, validating each threat natively on the cloud (AWS, GCP, or Azure) it was discovered against. Of 233 AI-discovered threats, 103 were confirmed and 34 refuted (75.2\% precision, 95\% CI [67.3, 81.7]); 44 were conditional (the named mechanism refuted but an equivalent impact shown through another path) and 52 indeterminate. Multi-model discovery helped through breadth, not agreement: the three models together found 2.2$\times$ the confirmed threats of the best single model at comparable precision, while threats reported by several models were confirmed no more often than single-model ones. False positives were not architecture-specific: they asserted access or system state the deployment did not have. Threats coded in advance as observable configuration resolved cleanly more often than multi-step behavioral threats (72.5\% vs.\ 51.6\%), which were more often conditional, suggesting that models more often misidentify the exploitation mechanism than the underlying weakness. AI-assisted discovery is a practical input to security workflows when paired with empirical validation.
events.title: Validating AI-Discovered Cloud Threats on Live Infrastructure: A Multi-Model, Multi-Cloud Study

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This technical report describes an alignment investigation into Mythos 5's behaviour during a security incident in UK AISI's cyber evaluations. During an evaluation, Mythos 5 attempted to execute a supply-chain attack against real people not involved in the evaluation task. Our investigation set out to understand the specific behaviour in this incident from an alignment perspective and identify broader lessons about failures of alignment. To do so, we conducted experiments in simulated replications of the original evaluation, and analysed model behaviour and reasoning when situated in the evaluation or asked questions about its scope. We find that, as in the original incident, Mythos 5 frequently reasons that the people it's targeting are simulated as part of the evaluation and provides invalid justifications for this conclusion. We also observe that Mythos 5 frequently attacks even in situations where, when directly asked, it states doing so would harm real people. While these issues are particularly prominent in Mythos 5, we find similar results in other models across providers. Our investigation suggests that models providing invalid justifications for their actions could make monitoring more difficult and complicate the analysis of misaligned behaviours observed in simulated environments, and we recommend model evaluators treat observations of undesired behaviour as important evidence of alignment failures even in the presence of simulation awareness in model reasoning.
events.title: Alignment Investigation of Mythos 5's behaviour in UK AISI's July 2026 Security Incident

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12480v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traditional communication resource allocation optimizes operational metrics such as rate, latency, energy efficiency, and reliability. Motivated by goal-oriented semantic communication, we develop a generalized allocation framework that transforms operational rewards through reference-dependent user utilities and evaluates them via expected utility, cumulative prospect theory (CPT), or related decision criteria. The formulation separates operational rewards, user-side valuations, and system-level decision criteria under uncertainty. We characterize utilities incorporating QoS/service reference levels, deficit sensitivity, post-reference saturation, and loss aversion. Weighted sum-reward maximization, proportional fairness, $\alpha$-fairness, and stochastic expected utility maximization emerge as exact special cases, while soft QoS-aware allocation follows from a deficit-penalty generalization. For deterministic orthogonal systems, we derive utility-weighted marginal-reward KKT conditions characterizing global optimality under concave composite objectives. For nonorthogonal and stochastic systems, we develop successive convex approximation (SCA) algorithms and establish stationary-point guarantees under explicit smooth and composite nonsmooth assumptions, including a CPT branch-stationarity result under eventual nondegenerate ordering identification. For globally solved penalized problems, we derive an $O(1/\lambda)$ bound on excess aggregate soft-QoS deficit, and on the deficit itself whenever a QoS-feasible allocation exist
events.title: Reference-Dependent Utility Optimization for Goal-Oriented Communication Systems

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. Designed for quorum-based systems, QUASI enables parties to attest to external entities that the statement is valid. Surprisingly, each party need not sign the entire statement: authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for the quorum to attest to the whole. A simple deterministic construction illustrates this possibility. Built purely from hashing and error correction, QUASI achieves small per-party contributions and low attestation generation and verification costs, without relying on SNARKs for aggregation. Our main contribution is a randomized construction achieving reductions of more than $10\times$ in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures. QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.
events.title: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern software systems routinely process credentials, personal records, and other sensitive information. A sensitive information exposure (SIEx) defect makes such information accessible to an unauthorized actor and can cause serious and often irreversible disclosure. However, prior research has focused largely on detecting such exposures rather than repairing the underlying defects, and existing repository-level issue-resolution benchmarks do not specifically target this defect class. We present SIExBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark dedicated to automated repair of SIEx defects. SIExBench contains 161 execution-verified instances from 64 widely used Python and Java repositories, each with an issue report, buggy repository snapshot, developer patch, executable exposure and regression tests, and defect characterization. We evaluate six repair systems with three LLMs, yielding 18 configurations, and systematically analyze their overall effectiveness, performance across defect characteristics, and failure mechanisms. The strongest configuration resolves only 39.1% of the instances, while 40.4% remain unresolved by all 18 configurations. More importantly, 62.1% of unsuccessful attempts produce a valid patch that still leaves sensitive information exposed, making incomplete exposure removal a central challenge. Systems often generate plausible patches and modify relevant code without fully eliminating the exposure, indicating that effective repair must ensure that all relevant paths to sensitive-information exposure are
events.title: SIExBench: A Benchmark for Automated Repair of Sensitive Information Exposure

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vector search on untrusted infrastructure exposes the \emph{query embedding}, a faithful summary of the user's intent. Fully homomorphic encryption can hide the query, but existing approaches still require a full scan followed by ranking of encrypted scores. Scalable private systems avoid encrypted ranking by either sending scores from a single cluster to the client or moving the search to the client, which must first stream the entire vector index for preprocessing. We present \textsc{Carousel}, which instead scores the full corpus under encryption and compresses the results for client-side ranking. The server scores every vector under encryption, raises the scores to a power that preserves their order by magnitude while suppressing all but a handful, and compresses the resulting sparse vector into a logarithmic number of ciphertexts using homomorphic additions alone. Because every vector is scored, \textsc{Carousel} incurs no recall loss from discarding candidates. Since clients hold no database-dependent state, insertions and deletions take effect immediately at the cost of a single vector write. \textsc{Carousel} searches $1$ billion vectors of BIGANN SIFT1B across multiple GPUs and achieves recall@100 of $0.9715$. At $100$ million SIFT vectors, it achieves recall@100 of $0.9845$ with a query latency of $3.735$ seconds on a single GPU.
events.title: CAROUSEL: GPU-Accelerated Private Vector Search via Homomorphic Sketching

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly execute consequential actions on behalf of users, but ordinary middleware guardrails do not provide cryptographic proof that a policy was actually enforced. Their verdicts leave counterparties dependent on the operator unless they repeat the checks themselves, potentially exposing sensitive policies and inputs. We present zkARc, a modular proof-carrying framework that wraps each stage of Automated Reasoning checks (ARc) in an independent, succinctly verifiable zero-knowledge proof. ARc is a neurosymbolic system that translates natural language policies into formal logic and verifies AI-generated content against them using SMT solvers. zkARc certifies the planner's output, the policy's formalization, the action's formalization and both solver queries. The receipt binds these computations to the exact action received and, under the stated assumptions, reveals no additional information about private policies and intermediate model values beyond the declared public information and verdict. This lets a third party check the claimed policy enforcement without re-running the pipeline or trusting the operator. We prove completeness, knowledge soundness and zero knowledge for the composed receipt under explicit assumptions. An implementation on Qwen2-0.5B enforces a spending policy end to end, approving two purchases and denying a third. A full receipt, which also proves model inference, takes about an hour to issue with CPU-only proving and verifies in under a minute, and the solver proof alone is 88 KiB
events.title: zkARc: Succinctly Verifiable Proofs for Neurosymbolic Natural Language Formalization and Verification

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12760v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern cyber threats commonly unfold as multi-step attacks comprising temporally and causally related phases. Current defenses commonly follow a detect first and correlate later paradigm. Intrusion detection systems classify events independently, while downstream systems reconstruct attack progression from the resulting alerts or audit records. In this context, learning-based detectors learn attack-step dependencies implicitly as statistical regularities in the data and cannot guarantee that their predictions follow the real attack progression. Conversely, correlation systems represent attack relationships explicitly, but apply this knowledge only after the underlying attack observations have been detected. We present DEEPCHRONOS, a neuro-symbolic network intrusion detection system that shifts the paradigm from detect first and correlate later to detection through logical progression. DEEPCHRONOS combines learned flow-level evidence with explicit attack-phase rules, temporal prerequisites, and previously inferred phases, allowing the evolving attack history to inform and constrain each detection decision. Evaluations on DARPA 2000 and AIT-LDS V2 show that DEEPCHRONOS improves macro F1 over purely neural baselines by up to 11.3%, eliminates causal violations under strict temporal constraints, and maintains millisecond-scale inference latency. These results demonstrate that integrating explicit attack progression knowledge into detection produces more accurate and temporally coherent multi-step attack predictions.
events.title: DeepChronos: Temporal Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Multi-Step Attack Detection

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CAPTCHAs can protect websites from malicious attacks. As a typical representative of behavior CAPTCHAs, slide puzzle CAPTCHAs have become increasingly popular in recent years due to their user-friendliness and high security. Previous attack methods on slide puzzle CAPTCHA mainly face challenges in the following four aspects. (1) The defense mechanisms of previous slide puzzle CAPTCHAs were relatively simple. The current slide puzzle CAPTCHAs have added complex interferences, detected slide trajectory features in the two-dimensional space, and added other defense mechanisms. (2) The previous notch detection methods were difficult to accurately locate the notch positions. (3) Previous attack trajectories were limited to the horizontal dimension, making them impossible to pass the existing detection. (4) The previous attack trajectories were generated by fitting functions, which were relatively simple and could not well simulate the slide characteristics of human users. In response to the above challenges, firstly, we systematically analyze the defense strategies of six most popular slide puzzle CAPTCHAs: Capy, Dingxiang, Geetest, Kyger, Shumei and Tencent. Secondly, for each type of CAPTCHA, we construct a notch detection dataset and a slide trajectory dataset separately. Thirdly, we use advanced YOLOv11 to detect the notch positions and train generative adversarial networks (GAN) to generate attack trajectories. As far as we know, we are the first to generate attack trajectories by directly learning human slide trajectory chara
events.title: Attacking Slide Puzzle CAPTCHAs Based on Time and Space Generative Adversarial Networks

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Immersive computing is poised to become a major paradigm for future human-computer interaction (HCI), enabling spatial and embodied experiences across applications such as education, healthcare, manufacturing, emergency response, and scientific discovery. However, today's Internet and computing infrastructure were not designed for real-time, multi-user, sensor-rich, and privacy-sensitive immersive applications. They require coordination across sensing, representation, compression, networking, edge/cloud computing, rendering, security/privacy, and human experience. This report summarizes key findings from the NSF Workshop on Networking and Systems Challenges in Immersive Computing. The workshop brought together researchers from networking, systems, extended reality (XR), artificial intelligence (AI), graphics, HCI, security, privacy, and applications to identify challenges and opportunities. We conclude that immersive computing cannot be enabled by isolated advances in network bandwidth, device capabilities, AI models, or rendering alone. The field needs end-to-end architectures that adapt to user behavior, application requirements, resource constraints, and social expectations. We organize the agenda into six themes: networked systems for immersive computing; real-time edge-cloud orchestration for XR applications; AI for immersive experiences; privacy, security, and trust in XR systems; human-centered design and user experience in XR; and scalable infrastructure, testbeds, and open ecosystems for XR. We further identify key re
events.title: Why Today's Internet Cannot Support Tomorrow's Immersive Experiences: Insights from the NSF Workshop

events.excerpt: arXiv:2510.11361v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a novel protocol that reduces worst-case packet latency in deflection-based on-chip interconnect networks. It enforces the deflection of the header of a packet but not its payload, resulting in a reduction in overall network traffic and, more importantly, worst-case packet latency due to decreased pre-injection latency.
events.title: A protocol to reduce worst-case latency in deflection-based on-chip networks

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Access-control policies are written in natural language but enforced as formal models, and translating them into NIST Next Generation Access Control (NGAC) graphs remains unsolved: prior systems cover only subsets of the NGAC model, and none verify the graphs they extract. We present Text2NGAC, a pipeline of cooperating large language models that disambiguates each sentence before extraction, escalates uncertain sentences to a multi-model ensemble, and checks the resulting graph with a five-strategy verifier whose own effectiveness is measured by controlled mutation testing. To our knowledge it is the first system to extract all four NGAC relationship types - associations, prohibitions, event-response obligations, and assignments - from real-world policy documents. Three results anchor the evaluation. The verifier detects 99.7% of 918 injected mutants and every structural fail-open fault, and the fault classes it misses are characterized and weighted by security consequence rather than left unexamined. The extracted graphs are enforceable: one corpus's graph loads unmodified into the NIST reference implementation, which reproduces all 55 access decisions the graph entails and fires an extracted obligation end-to-end. Extraction reaches 97.3-99.6% exact-tuple-match accuracy on the 714 scored sentences of four real corpora, far above three reproduced baselines on matched metrics, and paraphrase probes with semantic re-scoring bound the pipeline's sensitivity to rewording. Reported accuracy is wording- and benchmark-specific, adv
events.title: Text2NGAC: a multi-LLM pipeline for NGAC policy extraction with mutation-based verification

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information-flow control (IFC) is a promising approach to enforce policy in agentic AI systems. However, IFC suffers from label creep, a phenomenon where monotonically increasing security labels propagate through a system and progressively limit its utility. Label creep in agentic AI systems can be mitigated using two major strategies: (1) improved system design and (2) label declassification. In this paper, we characterize how far system design alone can mitigate label creep in agentic systems. Specifically, we measure how system topology, scale, and agent composition affect utility loss and security enforcement cost proxies for conservative IFC enforcement in a stateful agentic system simulator. We develop a pipeline to systematically vary these features and measure their impacts on label propagation. Our results demonstrate strong associations between structural graph features and our IFC utility loss metric (up to a Spearman correlation $|\rho|$ of $0.96$) and show that system size and tool allocation substantially affect how labels propagate. These findings identify design choices to reduce IFC utility loss, but they also demonstrate that system design alone cannot fully prevent utility loss due to monotonic label propagation. This motivates the development of label declassification mechanisms that aid these design choices and diminish IFC utility cost.
events.title: The Limits of Information-Flow Control Enforcement for Agentic Systems

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10638v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to decide where Internet of Things (IoT) tasks with different latency limits run in the edge-cloud continuum, yet some methods give every missed task the same penalty and few compare their agents with an optimal policy. This benchmark study builds four offloading systems small enough to solve exactly by dynamic programming and measures reward and learner against the optimum. A bonus for a met limit makes each miss cost its penalty plus the bonus, which shifts the class weights of published per-class rewards. A class-blind penalty stays 65% to 118% above the optimal cost even with a perfect learner, while a corrected per-class penalty comes within 0.13% of the optimum. With a per-class reward, tuned proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents come within 9% to 11% of the optimum in the smallest system, and the corrected one beats a tuned reservation rule in 9 of 10 seeds. In larger systems the agents stay 41% to 76% above the optimum, and a tuned rule beats their mean. Training ten times longer does not close this gap, and a PPO-Lagrangian agent with reachable targets does no better than the per-class reward.
events.title: SLA-Aware Task Offloading in the IoT Edge-Cloud Continuum: Class-Weighted Deep Reinforcement Learning Against an Exact Optimum

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Authorization of distributed energy resource (DER) commands judges a command by who sent it and whether its value has been seen before. An attacker holding a legitimate credential who writes ordinary values passes both tests. We add a check that judges each DER write against the grid's operating context: the bus voltages around the target, the hour, the day- ahead price, system load, and irradiance, compared with what operators wrote under similar conditions in the feeder's own benign history. We evaluate it live on the IEEE 123-bus and 8500-node feeders, driven by a measured 2024 year of price, load, and irradiance, against nine attack scenarios. A lookup trained on the same history catches none of the writes of the four scenarios that send values already familiar on the targeted device; the context check refuses 91.7% of insider-abuse writes and 64.4% of DER-aggregation writes while denying 1.28% of benign writes. In an offline test that replays recorded moments with curtailment setpoints drawn from the benign range, issued at a positive price, it refuses 47.3% and 50.5% on the two feeders, against 18.5% and 16.0% for the same check without context; live, the few setpoints tested were mostly shallow and were mostly allowed. The context check complements the lookup.
events.title: Checking DER Commands Against Grid Context Catches Credentialed Attacks Static Checks Miss

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12807v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is the standard paradigm for customizing large language models, yet third-party LoRA adapters pose a supply-chain risk: modifying less than 1% of model parameters suffices to implant stealthy backdoors. Recent defenses project adapter weights onto estimated backdoor subspaces, reporting near-zero static Attack Success Rates (ASR). We audit subspace-projection defenses across four model scales (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B) and three architectures (Qwen2.5, InternLM2.5, Spark). Constructively, module-wise rank-1 trigger-difference projection (k=1, alpha=1) reduces ASR from 60.4% to 0.0% on standard benchmarks and from 70.3% to 0.0% on a 1,000-sample uncontaminated suite (p = 3.055e-299, instruction-level p = 9.49e-16) in under 5 seconds end-to-end, and we prove via a spectral-gap bound why trigger-free calibration with benign polite suffixes aligns with u1(B) (median cosine 0.9048) and achieves 0.0% ASR without prior trigger knowledge. Our main contribution is a negative finding: static ASR reduction does not imply parameter erasure. Under 5-sample few-shot reactivation, every evaluated weight-editing defense rebounds (91.7%-100.0% ASR in 1 epoch for standard projections, Fine-Pruning, ANP, SVD truncation and Li & Kim's dual-end projection; 48.7% for our single-round dual variant), all reaching 100.0% by Epoch 2, with first-epoch loss up to 5.7x lower than training from scratch. Using an exact spectrum-preserving Haar orthogonal rotation control (Frobenius norm 10.0928 preserved to 1.70e-6) and N=1..6 cumu
events.title: Suppression Is Not Erasure: Mechanistic Analysis and Reactivation Boundaries of Subspace Projection for LoRA Backdoor Defense

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based coding agents are widely used to develop critical production software. Even though coding agents are known to occasionally write vulnerable code, there has not been any investigation into how code base vulnerabilities evolve over time under coding agent contributions. In this work, we close this gap by investigating whether and how vulnerabilities in existing code lead coding agents to introduce similar vulnerabilities in the code they write. We first evaluate coding agents on 96 tasks that require implementing a new backend application in a repository where other applications already exist. Second, we investigate repository-level code generation on 20 pairs of tasks in real C/C++ projects. In each task, the agent is asked to complete code critical to memory safety. We find that in both settings, insecure existing code leads to agents writing vulnerable code more often. In backend generation, insecure neighbors reduce the share of correct and secure implementations by 3.4% on average, and in C/C++ repository-level coding, the average gap between secure and insecure contexts reaches 35.4%. Prompting to follow existing code-style or to be careful about security increases, respectively decreases, how strongly agents propagate vulnerabilities, but neither stops them. When asked to explain their implementation choices, coding agents attribute them to following another code site in 76.5% of cases, even though they recognize the introduced vulnerability in 69.9% of cases. These findings show that agents use existing vulnera
events.title: Coding Agents Propagate Vulnerabilities in Code Bases

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems improve Large Language Model (LLM) responses by incorporating information from external knowledge bases. However, recent studies have shown that attackers can extract substantial portions of private knowledge bases from RAG systems through repeated querying. Yet, state-of-the-art extraction attacks either rely heavily on external LLMs to generate adversarial queries or require a large number of queries. In this paper, we propose SNAPRAG, a novel and cost-efficient attack for extracting RAG knowledge bases through adversarial perturbations. Our approach algorithmically generates adversarial queries without relying on external LLMs and allows for a strictly configurable query budget. In particular, SNAPRAG uses a discrete token-mutation algorithm to generate novel queries in a strict black-box setting. Our adaptive dissimilarity threshold calibration systematically forces queries into unexplored semantic regions of the target database, enabling extraction with fewer queries. Specifically, to extract half of the target knowledge base, our method requires up to 6.77$\times$ fewer queries than existing approaches. Furthermore, within a fixed query budget, our method recovers up to 96.9%, outperforming the closest approach by 7.7-19.9%. We further evaluate SNAPRAG against active defenses, where it remains the leading attack on four of five defended targets, achieving 50.7-96.3% extraction rate.
events.title: SNAPRAG: Cost-Efficient Knowledge Extraction Attack on RAG Systems via Adversarial Perturbations

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11689v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: DNS zone configuration errors are a frequent source of outages and frustration, particularly in combination with DNSSEC. Research has attempted to address the problem of zone configuration errors using formal methods, but existing proposals (i) only verify the absence of specific, known configuration errors, and (ii) do not consider DNSSEC. We present a new formal model of the DNS that covers most of DNSSEC, making it one of the most complete DNS models to date. In addition, we present a new tool, DecDNS, that performs a resolvability change-impact analysis of zone configuration updates using our model. We show that such a change-impact analysis can identify configuration errors without explicitly searching for them. We evaluate DecDNS both formally and empirically. We prove that DecDNS is sound and complete and show that its results agree with widely used DNS software. Finally, we explain how our approach can be integrated into operational practice, helping guide zone management in the real world.
events.title: Declarative DNS - Resolving Recursive Resolution

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The convergence of decentralized architectures integrating Machine Learning, Computer Vision and Low Power Wide Area Networks is increasingly becoming an integral part of our daily existence. Internet of Things serves as a real-time data conduit enhancing decision making via embedded technology and continuous data exchange. This paper explores the feasibility of Edge Computing as a foundational pillar in this evolving landscape. We experiment under real world, dynamic conditions, evaluate the technological aspects, strategies, process flows and key observations under the broad Edge Computing domain. Research pathways include Multi-access Edge topologies in future 6G networks, model quantization, and satellite-enhanced communication platforms. Additionally, a discussion is added supporting the advanced AI functionalities, including zero-shot learning, multi modal perception, and decentralized generative AI, thereby broadening the scope of intelligent applications across various domains. The significance and research objective of this study are threefold: (1) evaluation of LoRaWAN and satellite IoT communication strategies, (2) analysis of CV workloads on edge hardware and (3) future research directions where Edge Computing can support low-latency, energy-efficient and socially impactful IoT applications. By explicitly addressing these aspects, we aim to establish a clear link between the technological feasibility, ultimately with a practical and socioeconomic relevance.
events.title: Edge Computing for Computer Vision in IoT: Feasibility and Directions

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biometric identity systems for decentralized applications need credentials that resist repeated enrollment and support private, publicly verifiable authentication. Capture and large-scale private deduplication run off chain while smart contracts authorize issuance and use; these stages span distinct trust domains, and a correct verdict covers only the checked inputs and gallery snapshot. Without binding and state checks, concurrent enrollments can issue duplicate credentials from correct verdicts, while substituted inputs can authorize unrelated credentials. We present BioBind, a protocol whose four backend interface conditions bind the deduplication query, gallery insertion and issued commitment to one captured vector, authenticate gallery transitions, and require a sound uniqueness verdict valid at finalization. Its encrypted instance uses bound requests, stale-session rejection and committee-confirmed migration. Capture-bound zero-knowledge authentication links credential use to the enrolled template and a fresh device-originated probe bound to the challenge. We give a conditional multi-session composition argument under explicit capture, backend and cryptographic assumptions. A prototype using LFW face features rejects the tested composition attacks; its unlinkable authentication circuit uses 31,445 constraints and about 305,000 gas. An equal-public-field baseline quantifies the cost of verifiable matching: witness-plus-proving medians are 1.989 s versus 1.119 s with device-trusted matching. Separate tests of encrypted enr
events.title: BioBind: Binding Biometric Deduplication to Zero-Knowledge Authentication
