We solve this problem by introducing novel matrix factorizations based on logarithmic perturbations of the function $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-z}}$ studied in prior works, which may be of independent interest. The resulting algorithm has smooth error, and for any $\alpha > 0$ and $t\leq n$, it is able to privately estimate the sum of the first $t$ data points with $O(\log^{2}(t)(\log\log t)^{1+2\alpha})$ variance. It requires $O(t)$ space and amortized $O(\log t)$ time per round, compared to $O(\log(n)\log(t))$ variance, $O(n)$ space and $O(n \log n)$ pre-processing time for the nearly-optimal bounded-input algorithm of Henzinger et al. Empirically, we find that our algorithm's performance is also comparable to theirs in absolute terms: with optimized parameters, our variance is less than $2\times$ theirs for $t$ as large as $2^{32}$.
events.title: Private Continual Counting of Unbounded Streams

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the advancement of beyond-5G networks, privacy-preserving communication and secure computation face critical challenges due to the openness of wireless channels. Existing security mechanisms protect data transmission but fail to secure the computation process itself. In this paper, we propose a UAV-assisted secure computing framework that integrates Cheon Kim Kim Song (CKKS) fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) with multi-party secure computation (MPC). Leveraging UAV flexibility, our framework decouples key distribution from encrypted computation, enabling secure encrypted weighted aggregation (EWA), encrypted matrix multiplication (EMM), and encrypted decision tree (EDT) inference. Experimental results show that our framework outperforms existing schemes: for EDT, it supports floating-point operations and achieves better time efficiency than Brakerski-Fan-Vercauteren (BFV); for EMM, it demonstrates superior time and space efficiency compared to Brakerski-Gentry-Vaikuntanathan (BGV) and Somewhat Homo- morphic Encryption (SHE); while for EWA, it ensures high numerical precision and robustness across varying data length.
events.title: A Privacy-Preserving UAV-Assisted Secure Wireless Communication and Computing System Based on Fully Homomorphic Encryption

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12634v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12\Delta^\top F\Delta$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $\alpha^{0.63}$. Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence. We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.
events.title: How Far Does Second-Order Linear Response Predict Quantization Mismatch? Pre-Registered Measurements on Five Language Models

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection. To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests. We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.
events.title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the fram
events.title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12865v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1\% to 89.1\% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construct
events.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems increasingly appear in criminal investigations as tools, targets, and sources of evidence, yet AI forensics lacks a systematic account of the artifacts they produce: investigators often do not know which traces to look for, and for many traces they do find, no established analysis technique exists. In this paper we first developed the Forensic AI Life Cycle (FALC) that unlike other life cycle models shifts the focus onto the forensic artifacts created during the life cycle of an AI system. Through FALC we derived a reference list of artifacts that might serve an investigation. Second, we collected examples for crimes with AI involvement throughout FALC and questions likely to be asked when investigating these crimes. Third, we propose a taxonomy of forensic fields of expertise with a focus on the current possibility to analyze AI forensic artifacts using established techniques. For investigators, the model provides a systematic basis for identifying which artifacts to look for when an AI system is relevant to a case. For researchers, the classification shows where existing forensic methods already suffice and where new techniques are most urgently needed.
events.title: FALC: An Artifact-Centric Life Cycle Model and Research Agenda for AI Forensics

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study interactive proofs for arithmetic circuits over the complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ in which both the prover and the verifier compute approximately (unlike muggles, wizards can use magic, i.e., floating-point numbers). The goal is to prove that a claimed output $y$ is close to the exact output $C(x)$: for thresholds $0 \Delta$. Existing proof systems for real-valued data verify rounded finite-field computations. Bitan et al.~[EUROCRYPT~2026] gave an approximate sum-check protocol. We extend the protocol of Goldwasser, Kalai, and Rothblum (GKR) [STOC~2008] to public-coin interactive proofs for logspace-uniform layered circuits over $\mathbb{C}$ of size $S$, depth $L$, and $n$ inputs, under public bounds on gate values and wiring coefficients. At constant soundness error, the verifier runs in time $(n+1)\mathrm{poly}(L,\log S,b)$, the communication is $\mathrm{poly}(L,\log S,b)$, and the prover runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(S,b)$, where $b$ is the bit precision. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first doubly efficient interactive proofs in which both parties compute approximately. GKR reduces two claims about a layer to one on a random line, which leaves the unit circle, where our error bounds hold. We instead label gates by complex roots of unity and combine the two claims with a random root of unity as coefficient. We choose the error thresholds backward from the input layer, so that a large output error survives the verifier's rounding at every step. The honest prover needs only $O(S \log S)$ complex operations.
events.title: Delegating Computation with Approximate Arithmetic: Interactive Proofs for Wizards

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.
events.title: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, AI agents now take on paid work on-chain. The client locks the pay in an escrow, and the escrow pays the agent when the work is accepted. As this grows, each payment also has to cover others: a tax that funds public services, a fee to whoever referred the job, or the repayment of a loan the agent took to do the job. This is a draft ERC for Settlement Deductions . It lets an escrow withhold these amounts from each payout. The escrow does not need to know the rules behind them. None of them can stall the payout. It works for any task escrow, not only those used by agents. Example: a payout of 100, with a 1% tax, a 2% referral fee and a repayment of 30. The treasury gets 1, the referrer 2, the lender 30. The payee gets 67. Repository (draft text, reference policy, example escrow, tests): GitHub - unicore-gpu/settlement-deductions: Draft ERC: settlement deductions for task escrows (tax, premiums, repayments withheld at payout, never stalling settlement) · GitHub The ERC text is ERC-draft.md in the repository. I will open the PR to ethereum/ERCs next, with this thread as its discussion link. The slot this fills Escrows for agent work end in one transfer to the payee. The token-bound task tender draft (ERC-8414) pays the fulfiller on acceptance, verification or timeout. ERC-8183 releases the budget to the provider when the evaluator completes the job. But at that moment, others often have a claim on the money: A network may fund dispute resolution and monitoring with a small tax on settled work. An agent that referred the job may be owed a share of the pay. A lender
events.title: ERC: Settlement Deductions for Task Escrows

Japan, India, and Canada will get their turn in May. Schultz said Cisco is “working tirelessly” to deploy Cloud Control across the world as soon as possible. events.excerpt: Hi everyone, We built a prototype to see what it would take for a Zcash node to verify a STARK proof for an L2 batch. We wanted to measure the cost to the node and identify what a future transaction format would need to specify. STARK verification through Transparent Zcash Extensions (TZEs) was considered for NU7. The Zcash Foundation’s polling recap found insufficient support for including it and called for further discussion of the use case and design. NU7 shipped without a new transaction format. We ran our experiment on a separate local Regtest network with Zebra v7, NU7 rules, and an experimental transaction extension. NU7 polling recap · NU7 deployment specification What ran on Regtest We built a Rust verifier and integrated it into Zebra. A small Cairo token ledger uses the extension to submit batches. Each accepted batch spends the output that records the previous ledger state and creates a new one. Both nodes check the Stwo proof before accepting the transition. In two full test runs, both nodes accepted six chained batches per run. We tested deposit claims, L2 transfers, withdrawals, re-proving a batch after a reorg, and continuing after a node restarted from finalized state. The 4:45 demo follows four batches. With the sequencer stopped, we rebuild the ledger from on-chain data, generate a withdrawal proof, and mine the transaction. Zebra also rejects two variants before accepting the valid transaction. events.excerpt: Windows testers are getting a new option in the Sticky Keys and Filter Keys dialogs – one to banish the pop-ups without needing to venture deep into Settings. It's only taken several decades for Microsoft to put the off switch where the interruption actually happens. The accessibility features themselves are useful, though triggering their activation prompts by accident is another matter. Once enabled, Sticky Keys let users press modifier keys (such as Control) one at a time instead of holding them down together. For example, rather than holding Control and pressing C to copy, a user can press and release Control, then press C. Filter Keys, meanwhile, ignores brief or repeated keystrokes and adjusts the keyboard's repeat behavior. However, the dialogs are of little use to people who don't need the features, and they can pop up at the most inconvenient moments. Tap Shift five times, and you'll see what we mean: Windows chimes and shows a dialog asking whether you'd like to turn on Sticky Keys. Dismiss it, hit Shift five times, and there it is again. Or hold down the right Shift key for eight seconds to be treated to the Filter Keys pop-up. You can stop this behavior elsewhere in the system, but it requires a trek through Windows settings. The change, introduced in the Experimental Windows Insider Build 26340.9882, adds an option to the Sticky Keys or Filter Keys dialogs to dismiss the prompts permanently. It's a small change, but one that should spare users an irritating interruption. Better late than never – even if "never ask me again" has taken roughly three decades to re
events.title: Microsoft takes three decades to make Sticky Keys less sticky

events.excerpt: This is the discussion thread for EIP-8487 (PR: Add EIP: Separate execution credits and billing credits by Giulio2002 · Pull Request #12637 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub ). The proposal introduces two counters, both initialized from tx.gasLimit : Credits follow the legacy gas schedule and are the only gas the EVM sees (GAS opcode, call forwarding, creation). Billing follows the new schedule and determines the transaction fee. If billing runs out, the whole transaction aborts (uncatchable), even if credits remain. The goal is to let opcodes be repriced without changing execution behavior for contracts that inspect or forward gas. Open questions: the exact schedules, charge points, rebate rules, receipt fields and block accounting. Feedback welcome. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full topic

events.excerpt: Microsoft has unleashed a whopper of an update for Azure Linux, packing more than 470 CVE fixes into a single release as the software industry's ever-growing pile of vulnerabilities shows little sign of shrinking. Over the weekend, Microsoft rolled out Azure Linux 3.0.2022 with fixes covering everything from the Linux kernel to open source packages and container software. The changelog runs to hundreds of entries, so anyone planning to read the whole thing might want to put the kettle on. Microsoft's release notes contain more than 470 CVE references, although some vulnerabilities appear multiple times because they affect different packages. So that's not necessarily 470 separate security holes, but it's still an impressive amount of patching for one release. The fixes span OpenSSL, curl, Kubernetes, Docker, QEMU, and a lengthy list of other packages that underpin modern Linux environments. The generic Linux kernel has been updated to version 6.6.161.1. There's also been some housekeeping following the eMudhra certificate incident , tracked as CVE-2026-114406. Microsoft has removed or distrusted root certificates that could validate compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates, while adding checks in Python and Go to reject the affected certificates. It has also preserved SSL.com TLS trust where required, presumably to avoid fixing one certificate headache by creating another. events.excerpt: Toilet paper purveyor Who Gives A Crap has found itself in a bit of a mess after an intruder accessed customer information through a third-party software provider, leaving the company scrambling to clean up a breach affecting shoppers in the UK, US, and Australia. In an email sent to affected customers over the weekend, seen by The Register , the loo roll seller warns that personal information was accessed without authorization after a security incident at an unnamed US-based marketing software provider. The email explains that the intruder gained access to the supplier's systems on October 30. The provider spotted the intrusion the following day and says it secured its systems by November 1, although Who Gives A Crap wasn't told until November 6. It's unclear why the supplier sat on the bad news for another five days before passing it on. The exposed information includes customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, and total spending with the company. In other words, someone may now know not only where you live, but just how much of your hard-earned cash you've flushed down the crapper. Payment information, order details, and passwords were not involved, and customers' accounts were not directly accessed. That's something of a relief, although whether the intruder actually made off with the data remains a pressing question. "We don't yet know whether the information was copied or downloaded," the company told customers, adding that it had found no evidence of misuse. events.excerpt: The AI bubble isn't about to burst, Forrester reckons, although businesses should prepare for a correction that could upend their suppliers, contracts, and prices. Spending on infrastructure has raced ahead of measurable returns, the analyst says, yet the financial strength of the companies funding the build-out is what keep Forrester from predicting an imminent crash. "Fears that an AI bubble is about to burst are premature," said Forrester emerging technology veep Brian Hopkins. "About nine-tenths of the money building today's AI computing infrastructure comes from large, healthy technology companies paying out of their own cash flow. The risk is concentrated in a few places: a small number of builders under real financial strain, and circular financing deals with the AI labs." Conveniently, Forrester has developed an AI Bubble Model to help technology leaders monitor the risks and prepare. Its latest report, " An AI Bubble Burst Is Not Imminent ," notes what many in the IT industry, including The Register , have been saying for a while: that the hyperscale operators are committing a record share of revenue into capital expenditure to bring online more infrastructure to support AI development and use. At the same time, the boost in productivity doesn't justify this supplier capacity build-out. Forrester calculates that the infrastructure investments break even only if AI raises US GDP by 5 percent by 2035. Published estimates suggest productivity improvements could provide about two percentage points of that uplift, leaving roughly $1.3 trillion to come from other sources
events.title: The AI bubble can wait, but your exit plan can't

events.excerpt: A validation error has stopped Outlook.com from accepting legitimate emails. The problem appears widespread and, according to reports from affected users, can result in non-delivery reports with error codes related to SPF (Sender Policy Framework) validation failures. Other users have reported errors highlighting a lack of DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) information. The troubles began at the end of last week and appear to be the result of Microsoft tightening the rules (or at least attempting to do so) for accepting emails. The company's consumer email services are affected, and it appears that if a domain doesn't have working SPF or if it has a missing DMARC record, then Outlook.com and its ilk will treat it as suspicious and not accept emails. The rules are designed to deal with spam, bulk senders, and the like. In 2025, Microsoft announced new rules designed to strengthen email authentication for domains sending more than 5,000 emails per day. In addition to DMARC and SPF compliance, DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) was also required . Although this seemed like a good idea to ward off spammers, small senders now appear to be affected. According to complainants in the Outlook forum, a single email with just one line might now be rejected. Furthermore, Microsoft has not issued any advisory to customers explaining how the rules have changed. events.excerpt: "AI delusion" remains loosely defined, but most of us know it when we see it: exaggerated faith in the technology's power, applicability, or nature, coupled with a refusal to acknowledge its limitations. It's bad in the individual, as when an elderly relative emails you a hallucination-laden ChatGPT summary. It's worse in management, when your boss insists that AI slop is genius marketing content at a bargain rate. It is terrifying in tech CEOs. It is not, thankfully, compulsory. Consider three recent examples of technology leadership in the age of AI. One would be Pythonesque were the disconnect with engineers and the public not so profound. Another risks becoming a business-school case study in how to demolish customer trust. The third offers something less fashionable: robust pragmatism. Saving the best till last, y'all. Case 1: we present for your consideration Sam Altman of OpenAI, one of the few actually at the controls of the singularity machine. It seems churlish to pluck just one luscious fruit out of that cornucopia of choices, yet we must. Sam Altman thinks it is a sin against the natural order that so much RAM is idling in machines owned by individuals, organizations, and anywhere that isn't Big AI . It's oh so inefficient. How convenient that the efficient allocation of scarce resources should favor the business he runs. Free market schmarket. events.excerpt: A Welsh music enthusiast has built an internet radio station that plays AI-generated tunes alongside human-made tracks without telling listeners which is which, to find out whether listeners really hate AI music or just the idea of it. AI Slop FM is the creation of Mike Chaffin, who built and runs the station single-handedly from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire. By stripping away artist names, cover art, and any mention of AI, Chaffin hopes to find out what listeners really think when they have nothing but the music to go on. The free 24/7 station asks listeners to rate tracks from S to E, tag how the music makes them feel, and leave written feedback. The most popular submissions will eventually make it into a weekly chart called the Slop 40, giving creators something that can be hard to come by in the age of streaming: an actual audience. Anyone can submit a track, including human musicians, although Chaffin has already discovered that not all of them are particularly keen on the idea. He told The Register that he had floated the idea to an unsigned musician friend who had sold around 600 albums, but was met with a rather nervous response. "Wh, wh, why would I want to do that?" the musician reportedly asked, according to Chaffin, who said he had never heard his friend stutter before. "It seems that there is a deep rooted fear of AI music in the industry," Chaffin said. The station is still in beta, with Chaffin waiting for enough submissions to fill its schedule across different genres before opening it fully. He's already been pleasantly surprised by the quality of the music s
events.title: AI Slop FM radio experiment puts machines on trial, one dodgy tune at a time

events.excerpt: Rising memory prices are pushing more customers toward refurbished tech, suppliers say, with warranties of up to three years helping to make secondhand kit a less daunting purchase. Memory costs have more than quadrupled this year as manufacturers prioritize more lucrative high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for servers powering AI datacenters. Many enterprises are keeping equipment longer in an uncertain economy. Ben Caddy, senior analyst at Omdia, said suppliers were linking refresh discussions with opportunities to recover value from customers' aging kit. By 2030, he predicted, 35 percent of "all the hardware sold for the channel will be taken back by partners," driven "by the sheer economic logic of taking equipment back, recovering value, and embracing more circular IT lifecycles." This is already helping some customers "unlock some capital to put towards those [relatively] small refresh plans," he said while hosting a panel on circular IT at last month's Canalys Forums in Barcelona. Refurbished smartphones are growing in popularity, but persuading customers to trade in their old devices remains a constraint on supply. The same applies to PCs and other equipment, said Jon Sansom, MD at GreenSafe IT. "Availability is a challenge," he said. events.excerpt: Today I am excited to announce Veylor, a new Zcash wallet which allows you to self custody shielded USDC. It uses USDC shielded in Railgun on Ethereum (0zkUSDC) and a trustless, atomic bridge to swap to and from shielded ZEC. Both the wallet and the bridge are open source and run on mainnet today in a capped beta. So how does this it work? The Bridge The bridge works similarly to an HTLC, where it uses Ethereum’s programmability to escrow the USDC, while the ZEC is held under a spending key that is split between two parties. The contract on Ethereum implements the Pallas elliptic curve and takes advantage of two properties: Given a public point ( E = e·G ) you cannot recover the secret ( e ) used to generate it. The public key of the sum of two secrets is the sum of their public keys: E + Z is the public key of e + z . So both sides can derive the joint ZEC address from E and Z , without anybody holding its full spending key. The flow: The user and the bridge agree on a quote and exchange the public keys of their secrets, each with a proof that they know the secret. The user also sends the bridge the Railgun note the 0zkUSDC must be paid to. The bridge then locks the USDC in the escrow contract under both public keys, two deadlines (t0 and t1) and the user’s payout note. The wallet independently verifies the escrow on Ethereum, waits 3 blocks, and then sends the ZEC to a fresh shielded address whose spending key is e + z . Both sides derive this address from E + Z . Once the ZEC has 2 confirmations, the bridge marks the swap as ready in the contract. This gives up its right
events.title: Veylor: A New Zcash Wallet with a Shielded Atomic Bridge

events.excerpt: Can an IBM Z mainframe run Doom? Of course it can. The more interesting question is whether you can play it through a text terminal without ruining your eyesight. WND Software's browser demo connects to an IBM Z mainframe over SSH using its terminal emulator. Wojciech Graj's DOOM-ASCII supplies the text-based carnage, replacing conventional graphics with colored characters. There's no sound. It is, however, completely playable (although you might need to recalibrate your vision to work out what is going on, particularly with regard to distant objects). Sessions are limited to five minutes, with room for up to 50 simultaneous users, but we had no trouble getting in. ASCII also presented no issues once the game was in motion. This writer played the original shareware release on an Amstrad ALT386SX portable, so squinting at an indistinct demon felt reassuringly familiar. That Doom can be persuaded to run on an IBM Z mainframe is not particularly noteworthy. The code has turned up everywhere from databases to PCB designers . Even the humble Pi Pico was roped into the fun. Keeping the action playable through a text terminal is the more entertaining achievement. A year ago, an IBM consultant persuaded Doom to run on IBM Z and LinuxONE using VNC to bring the pixelated mayhem to life. Using a terminal emulator, while a neat demonstration of the capabilities of WND's software, is perhaps more an example of "because I can" masochism. It's undeniably an enjoyable way to burn through five minutes. No installation or login required – just a willingness to shoot at punctuation. ®
events.title: Doom delivers five minutes of terminal violence on an IBM mainframe

events.excerpt: The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) kicks off its quadrennial plenipotentiary on Monday, and internet governance organizations are bracing in case the event becomes a forum for nation-states to try to challenge their roles. The ITU is the United Nations' specialized agency for information and communication technologies, meaning its members are nation-states. The body's role is to facilitate international connectivity, which it does by managing radio spectrum, satellite orbits, and working on relevant technical standards. Its key standards are pervasive. ITU-T X.509 sets out the rules of public key infrastructure. ITU-T E.164 governs telephone numbers. ITU-T H.264 and 265 define the video codecs used for most online streams. The ITU's role is largely uncontested, yet its work gets very close to that of the organizations who work on technologies that make the internet work. Those bodies include the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF); the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), which oversees the domain name system; and the regional internet registries (RIRs), which manage IP addresses. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) works on HTML, CSS, and accessibility. Governments participate in work at those internet governance bodies but are just one voice among many and can't override the consensus-driven decision-making process they use, under a system which has come to be known as the multi-stakeholder governance model. At a 2025 event called WSIS+20, the United Nations endorsed multi-stakeholder governance by deciding that its Internet Govern
events.title: Internet governance about to get its quadrennial stress test at ITU meeting

events.excerpt: In October 2025, Vitalik’s GKR tutorial was my first encounter with GKR. Its central observation, that the protocol commits only to a circuit’s input and output and never to the layers in between, made GKR look like the natural tool for proving hash-heavy computation. A year later, that has led to what is, as far as we know, the first machine-checked soundness bound for GKR on general layered circuits, in Isabelle/HOL. The same work produced a soundness proof for sparse-Merkle updates built on that bound, a partial refinement that ties the model to the Rust code, and a sparse prover whose release 1.2 proves 2.41–2.71× faster with byte-identical proofs and unchanged Isabelle theories. This post follows that work, StateSync-GKR, from the protocol and its field to the update a circuit encodes, the Rust code and the prover arithmetic. Two arXiv papers give the details: Soundness of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates, with a Machine-Checked Core and StateSync-GKR: Design and Evaluation of a Reusable Sparse GKR Engine , whose appendix plots the measurements in 363 panels. All formal results are proved in the first paper, and Isabelle/HOL also checks the parts marked as machine-checked. The main results: The first machine-checked GKR soundness bound for general layered circuits, with a cube gate. For circuits with linear, product and cube gates, Isabelle/HOL checks the bound (s_out + Σᵢ(2sᵢ·db(sᵢ) + 1))/|𝔽| for the whole layer chain and any layer polynomial of total degree at most db(sᵢ), on top of the sumcheck formalization in the Archive of Formal Proofs (dates in Sectio
events.title: GKR with a Machine-Checked Core, and a Sparse Prover Made Faster with Byte-Identical Proofs

events.excerpt: Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so. Ferguson told The Register in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics." The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital. "You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said. For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said. "The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. You are always better routing between a few models than to do one singular model." That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. As a managed inference platform, Fireworks AI routes inference tasks to whichever model, frontier model subscription, or API is best suited to handle them. But the company is not just doing naive routing like an AI gateway. It's eva
events.title: Fireworks says you’re wasting money on AI unless you’re using all the models

events.excerpt: NHS staff drafted into a helpline after colleagues' health data was exposed online faced distressed callers, safeguarding concerns, and a "serious emotional impact," a review has found. The report [PDF] comes almost exactly a year after the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust disclosed a data breach affecting 8,003 people, including current and former trust staff and non-trust workers. A member of the public discovered the exposure in November 2025. An Excel workbook published in response to a Freedom of Information request in February 2023 retained underlying sickness absence records that users could reveal through its pivot tables. Staff assigned to the helpline described difficult calls involving shouting, anger, and distress. Particularly difficult calls involved people distressed by the sensitivity of the disclosures or potentially in danger from domestic abuse. Call handlers said they had to make safeguarding assessments without training or an established process. "Such occurrences of anger or distress were not infrequent, and this reflected the heightened emotions and distress experienced by callers to varying degrees due to the breach," the review noted. "This placed significant emotional burden on individuals working in the contact center, who were not prepared or provided support on how to deal with those." Members of the trust's clinical governance team were told just a day beforehand that they would staff the helpline. Despite their experience dealing with patient trauma, they received little preparation for the calls that followed. "The staff working in the call
events.title: NHS breach helpline left staff carrying a 'significant emotional burden'

events.excerpt: Hi Optomism, I’m [Your Name], a smart contract and zkVM protocol developer. I’ve been building BitcoinMerkleVerifier_ZK , a gas-optimized, zero-knowledge verification infrastructure designed to bring trustless Bitcoin interoperability directly to Optomism. The Problem We Solve: Existing cross-chain bridges rely on trusted multisig federations or vulnerable oracles, while running raw Bitcoin Merkle tree traversals and double-SHA256 loops on-chain is cost-prohibitive. Our Solution: Our protocol offloads heavy cryptographic Bitcoin Merkle path calculations off-chain into an SP1/RISC Zero zkVM guest program, submitting a compact ~192-byte Groth16 proof to the EVM contract. This slashes verification costs down to a flat ~200k gas while ensuring bulletproof security backed by OpenZeppelin circuit breakers ( Pausable ) and multi-sig governance. Why [Optimism]? Deploying this infrastructure on Optomism directly expands your ecosystem’s TVL by unlocking trustless Bitcoin-backed assets, cross-chain yield protocols, and BTCFi applications with maximum cryptographic security. Current Status & Deliverables: Smart contracts and Foundry test suites fully implemented. zkVM Rust guest program structured and optimized. Seeking [$5000 / Support] to fund our upcoming testnet deployment, security audit, and mainnet launch. I would love to share our technical documentation and GitHub repository with you. events.excerpt: A roadside display at Cherwell Valley services has stopped dispensing information and started asking for help. The eagle-eyed Register reader who spotted the stricken screen told us: "UK motorway signs often tell us that tiredness can kill, urging us to take a break. This poor thing at Cherwell Valley services took the advice to heart." The display at the Moto services appears to have run into trouble during a restart. Windows offers another attempt or access to repair tools, although the latter options are hidden – perhaps somewhere on the top floor of the neighboring Travelodge. Getting things moving again will probably require access to the computer behind the screen. The Automatic Repair screen is all too familiar to Windows users. Not to be confused with the classic blue screen of death, it might indicate a misbehaving driver during a reboot, an update that did something unexpected, or some sort of hardware failure. Hopefully it isn't the latter – with memory and storage prices the way they are at the moment, a motorway services sandwich or gallon of fuel will seem a positive bargain by comparison. Our reader is right: taking a break is sensible advice. Getting Windows to end one can be another matter. ®
events.title: Windows takes a break at UK motorway services

events.excerpt: TL;DR: An opt-in, public, per-account “protected” flag for ERC-20s. Small sends stay instant; anything bigger is scheduled and can be cancelled by a pre-registered backup wallet; a “stress” action sweeps everything to the backup and locks it, which also helps against wrench attacks. Turning protection on is instant; weakening it (off, higher limit, shorter waits, new backup) takes a delay the holder picks. Why: Today a stolen key or a coerced holder means an instant, final drain. Existing approaches are per-transfer (SLOW), need recipient cooperation (ERC-8236), need judges (ERC-20R), protect protocols rather than users (ERC-7265), or only work in one smart wallet. This puts the protection in the token, so it works for any holder and any wallet, including plain EOAs. How it works: protect(backup, dailyLimit, holdWindow, offDelay, lockDuration, fastLane) : instant. Over-limit transferFrom reverts (never returns true without moving tokens, so routers, vaults and lenders can’t be fooled). Over-limit transfer from an EOA may be auto-scheduled, so wallet “Send” buttons just work. queueTransfer → hold window → anyone can executeTransfer ; the owner or backup can cancelTransfer ; with the opt-in fast lane, the backup can approveTransfer to skip the wait. stress(account) : cancels everything pending and moves the balance to the backup, locked for a preconfigured duration (the caller can’t choose it, so a coerced caller can’t pick zero). Receiving is always instant; unprotected accounts are plain ERC-20. Status: We built a working reference implementation at ETHGlobal Mumbai: a 1:1
events.title: ERC-XXXX: Protected Accounts for Fungible Tokens--*

events.excerpt: Description Clean builds of sui-node are slow: about 164s in dev and about 296s in release on a 16-core Mac. This cuts them to about 130s in dev and about 231s in release without removing functionality. Each commit stands alone: Drop unneeded crates from the graph. sui-simulator re-exported Move package and build crates that nothing used. These pulled move-compiler and sui-sdk into the build. sui-indexer-alt-metrics now puts its postgres collector behind a postgres feature, so diesel and postgres are no longer built. No host build of sui-types for a build script. sui-package-management 's build.rs now reads the snapshot manifest JSON directly instead of depending on sui-framework-snapshot . Less code generation in sui-core . Spawn helpers box futures before tokio::spawn , so tokio compiles one task harness instead of one per future type. This costs one extra allocation per spawn. typed-store 's DBMap / SafeIter methods move the code that doesn't depend on the key and value types into non-generic functions. SuiNode::start_async returns a boxed future, so node startup compiles once in the sui-node library instead of again in the binary. rocksdb no longer waits for jemalloc. rocksdb's jemalloc feature only enables jemalloc's unprefixed malloc. The C++ define it adds isn't read by rocksdb's sources. typed-store now turns on that jemalloc feature directly, so rocksdb's C++ build script starts without waiting for jemalloc's. The resolved jemalloc features are the same as before. Test plan Covered by existing tests for the changed crates. Timings come from alternating clean cargo
events.title: sui_v1.85.0_1794023194_ci: Speed up clean builds of sui-node (#28560)

events.excerpt: How large can EIP-8141’s validation budget be? A mempool DoS benchmark Authors: Stefano De Angelis , Daniil Ankushin , Manuel Arto . All at Nethermind. Thanks to Thomas for feedback and comments on the initial benchmarking plan . TL;DR EIP-8141 caps unpaid validation at MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 100k; too low for a Groth16 privacy transfer or post-quantum signatures . Raising the cap is a DoS risk, since validation and block processing share the node’s CPU. An attacker can send transactions that use the whole cap and then fail, taking CPU from block processing for free. We tested this risk on a Nethermind node, flooding it with such transactions at caps from 100k to 500k, on one CPU core (the worst case) and three machines. Without in-client protections, block processing on our slowest machine stays within a 25 ms delay budget only up to 15M gas/s. With Nethermind allowing up to about 100 failing tx/s per connection, that limits the cap to the current 100k. We show that a MAX_VERIFY_GAS = 300k is viable with an in-client protection that pauses transaction validation while the node processes a block. At 100 tx/s (30M gas/s), block processing then stays within 50 ms, even on p90 mainnet blocks. The cost moves to the mempool, which admits only 12–27% of honest frame transactions under the flood. 1. Introduction In an ordinary Ethereum transaction the signature check is cheap and fixed. In an EIP-8141 frame transaction the check is arbitrary EVM code in a VERIFY frame. Before admitting the transaction to its mempool, a node simulates its validation prefix , the frames up to and includin

events.excerpt: ML admins will be happy to learn that one bad GPU may no longer mean starting an entire training job from scratch. The latest 2.15 release of PyTorch includes a rewritten backend for Nvidia's Collective Communications Library (NCCL), designed to improve fault diagnosis and recovery when GPUs work together. This latest feature shows how its creators continue to advance the software from being a tool for researchers to being a cornerstone in production AI work. The interface to the networking library in PyTorch needed a rewrite – it was drowning in technical debt, said PyTorch core developer Tristan Rice , a Meta software engineer specializing in distributed computing, during a live YouTube livestream on Thursday. NCCL is pronounced "Nickel" and stands for the Nvidia Collective Communications Library. It provides PyTorch with a set of inter-GPU communication primitives, allowing GPUs to communicate within a single-node or across multi-node clusters, which is vital for running inference on large neural networks and for other tasks in building and maintaining LLMs. The old NCCL interface was too chaotic The previous PyTorch backend for NCCL, called ProcessGroupNCCL , could spawn dozens of communicators per process group, leading to intermittent deadlocks and unpredictable performance. The new version of the NCCL backend comes with a strict rule: One process group gets only one communicator during initialization. By default, this rule eliminates crosstalk between multiple communicators and all the complexities that entails. If a program requires parallelism, it will have to disp
events.title: PyTorch 2.15 tackles the 'one bad GPU' problem

events.excerpt: Linux can do many things, but good looks aren't always its strong point. Apple has rather more of a reputation in that department, and a crop of new projects is bringing Mac-style polish to the open source desktop. Some are all-new, such as the Argentinian Lord OS , a whole new GUI desktop on top of Debian. Another, Cutefish , is a revival of a pre-ChatGPT project that never got as far as a complete release. Now it has version 1.0 for both x86-64 and Arm64, plus it's working on Mac binary compatibility via a work-in-progress layer called Reef . Ukrainian Desert OS is already at version 5.5 – practically a venerable elder in this company, despite appearing to be only about a year old. Meanwhile, ClokeOS uses Xfce for its desktop, but underneath, the OS is based on Apple's FOSS XNU kernel. The project lead plans to offer compatibility with multiple types of binaries: Linux apps, plus Mac apps via Darling , and Windows apps via Wine. This isn't new. Much as Cutefish has been revived, last year we reported on PearOS Linux , a very Mac-like skin on KDE Plasma. It has hooks in place for ambitious future features, such as Siri-style speech recognition. What's striking is the number of projects appearing and the pace of their development. Some offer both x86-64 and Arm64 builds, with Raspberry Pi editions in certain cases. For human coders, this would be months of hard work, but if it's just checking an additional box in an LLM development tool, then why wouldn't you? It's almost no extra work, but it widens the potential audience. Coveting Mac-like good looks is a longstanding urg
events.title: Mac lookalikes multiply as Linux raids Apple's wardrobe

events.excerpt: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) now boasts a system for research into quantum error correction, combining IBM quantum processors with a high-performance compute (HPC) system based on AMD silicon. The Quantum Science Center ( QSC ) at ORNL, funded by the US Department of Energy (DoE), unveiled what it calls a co-design platform for quantum error correction, marrying up quantum and HPC technology. While useful, fault-tolerant quantum systems always seem to be at least a decade away, there have been notable advances over the past several years in the field of quantum error correction, according to ORNL. These include early demonstrations of protecting quantum information from environmental noise, which can cause loss of the fragile quantum states needed for computations. "Solving the challenges of quantum error correction is essential to making quantum computing a practical tool for scientific discovery, which is a priority for Oak Ridge National Laboratory," said QSC director Travis Humble. IBM Fellow and director of IBM Research Jay Gambetta said that it was no longer a question of whether error correction works, but how to accelerate and optimize error correction to build systems that scientists can use to tackle challenging problems. "This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software and workflows that will scale," he stated. ORNL's new tool combines an IBM Quantum System Two, equipped with the latest 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 quantum processors , and Umbra, a classical HPC system
events.title: Oak Ridge labs gets hybrid quantum-HPC system to test qubit error correction

events.excerpt: Elon Musk has hit the brakes on the Cybertruck, announcing on X that Tesla will wind down production at its Texas factory around mid-2027. Despite years of delays , the stainless-steel turd Musk claimed was a futuristic, apocalypse-proof tank straight out of Blade Runner is headed for a production wind-down after roughly four years, putting the Cybertruck alongside such automotive flops as the Edsel and the DeLorean. We can’t even put the Cybertruck on the same tier as the Ford Pinto, as that deathtrap was produced for a decade. The first Cybertruck lumbered off Tesla’s production line in mid-2023 before going on sale later that year , and it was practically right out of the gate that the problems began. Within months of the first deliveries, recall notices began piling up on the monstrosity. Trim pieces were flying off, internal components were failing, cameras were malfunctioning – all in all, the thing has faced 11 recalls since hitting the road in late 2023, most recently in April 2026, when a defect in brake rotors was found to potentially cause cracks that could allow wheel studs to separate from their hubs. Musk had pinned a lot of Tesla's hopes on the Cybertruck a few years ago, describing it during the company's Q3 2023 earnings call as "a great product" that would eventually generate "significant positive cash flow" for Tesla. Musk said on that same earnings call that Tesla intended to ramp Cybertruck production up to 250,000 vehicles per year by 2025 to meet the over one million Cybertruck reservations he claimed Tesla had taken. Some Musk fans may still be waiti
events.title: RIP to the world’s ugliest car

events.excerpt: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) says its Super Intelligence Task Force (SINTF) is now up and running, after president Donald Trump ordered the move in a memo last month. Headed up by director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as associate attorney general Stanley Woodward and associate deputy attorney general Stephen Weiss, SINTF's responsibility is to protect the US's lead in artificial intelligence development. Thursday's announcement, which was littered with the " super intelligence " Trumpism, said the task force will ensure the US's SI/AI leadership remains uncompromised by foreign AI "abuse," including by state and state-backed groups, criminal enterprises, individuals, or corporate entities. Per Trump's October 13 memo [PDF], SITF will take "affirmative measures, as appropriate," to ensure the US stays ahead in AI development. It did not elaborate on what this nebulous phrase meant, but it can be reasonably assumed this means a breadth of proactive steps. The memo also stated that the task force will organize the DoJ's criminal and civil lawsuits involving AI, recommend enforcement priorities concerning public safety and AI misuse, develop prosecution guidance for unlawful AI conduct, and feed into legislative proposals to prevent "burdensome regulation." Addressing a Wall Street Journal tech conference this week, Pentagon CTO and SITF vice chair Emil Michael said the team would release details about its AI regulatory landscape later this month. The task force will also shoulder various cross-departmental responsibilities, such as "deconflicting invest
events.title: DoJ's 'Super Intelligence Task Force' up and running

events.excerpt: Daniil Ankushin, Nethermind. Verify-budget figures: method by Daniil Ankushin, benchmark and measurements by Manuel Arto. On frame transactions a shielded pool pays its own gas, so a private withdrawal needs no relayer. We ran a real BN254 Groth16 pool this way on current Nethermind master: a withdrawal costs 679,322 gas. With EIP-8250 nonce keys, many withdrawals can come from the one pool address at once. Two things do not work yet. The proof check is over the spec cap on validation gas, and a pool cannot pay for a call from the user’s own address. The pool we ran is soispoke’s minimal-shielded-pool ( GitHub - soispoke/minimal-shielded-pool · GitHub ). How a withdrawal works In a withdrawal the pool is the sender. Its VERIFY code checks the zk proof and approves execution and payment. The user needs no funded account and does not appear in the transaction. Two drafts make this safe in a public mempool. With EIP-8250 the pool uses the note’s nullifiers as nonce keys. Each withdrawal has its own nonce key, so withdrawals with the pool as sender do not compete for one nonce. A side effect: a nullifier that was already used is a used nonce key, so the protocol refuses a double spend before the pool’s code runs. With EIP-8272 the transaction checks the pool’s Merkle root against a contract of recent roots before the pool’s code runs, so a mempool node never reads the pool’s storage. What it costs All values are from mined receipts on Nethermind master 4bcb9e30, single node. Step Gas Deposit a note, frame tx 990,503 of which state gas 195,840 Deposit a note, plain EIP-1559 call
events.title: A privacy pool on frame transactions: what works, and the case that does not yet

events.excerpt: Last week’s security notice on the Fearless Wallet browser extension ( notice ) says that from February 2025, unlocking the wallet sent your private key to a server run by the attacker. The notice links a write-up that walks through the code at fixed commits ( write-up ). I read it and then went through the repo history myself. None of it was hidden. It sat in public source the whole time. I audit smart contracts, not browser extensions, but the review lessons carry over to any code that touches keys. Like the write-up, I’m sticking to what the code and the history show, not who wrote it or why. How it got in, and how it left The code arrived in PR #1022 of soramitsu/fearless-wallet-web, titled “Ton Service”. It was open for ten weeks and merged on 19 February 2025 as one squashed commit, “TON ecosystem”: 251 files, 4,690 lines added and 6,119 removed. The PR has no review comments. The function that matters is about 25 lines, in a new 180 line file, inside a diff of almost 11,000 changed lines whose title says it adds TON. It left the same way. The code was deleted from the source on 25 June 2026, inside a release commit with about 80,000 changed lines. What each piece looked like in a diff The name. On every unlock the extension calls fetchJettonInfo() . Jettons are TON tokens, so in a TON PR that reads like a token info fetch. What it actually does is export the recovery phrase of every main account (or the keystore file plus the wallet password) and send it out. The password. The keyring service keeps the typed password in this.password at unlock. That’s what lets later

events.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture. The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That

events.excerpt: Hi all. We recently opened a discussion in the Solana SIMD repository about a new class of smart contracts we’re loosely calling “inference programs,” or “Actually Smart Contracts.” We’d value technical input from this community on whether a similar proposal could be feasible on Ethereum, before we write anything for it. The idea, briefly: a contract stores a prompt and the rules that shape it (a DAO constitution, a policy, a standard). Another contract asks it a question with evidence. AI models from different operators answer off chain, each signs a vote, and the caller checks the signed result before acting. The motivator was Anthropic’s recent work on zero-knowledge proofs of LLM inference . The Solana drafts and the discussion so far: Overview and drafts: Bringing Inference Programs To Solana Microsite with diagrams and a sandbox: asc.verafy.ai Discussion: solana-improvement-documents #724 We have no strong view on whether this is technically feasible, and we know there is a lot of prior work here that we may not have accounted for, including optimistic oracles and opML. The drafts were written with help from AI tools, so some of it may be poorly reasoned. The questions we’d most like help with: Is this better as an application-level ERC, or not a standard at all? Proofs of inference are currently far too large to verify on chain (about 18.78 MB each). Is a commit, bond and challenge design the realistic path on Ethereum, or is there a better one? What existing work should we build on or defer to instead? Thank you for any pointers. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full t

events.excerpt: Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change. An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document. GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works: Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance. New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work. events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. This enables a single implementation to coordinate callback-driven execution using different programs and calldata without deploying a new contract for each execution. Motivation Many advanced execution strategies require dynamically changing execution logic, particularly when interacting with external contracts that invoke callbacks during execution. Traditionally, dynamically changing the execution logic of a contract may require deploying a new contract containing the desired runtime code. This introduces deployment costs, including contract creation and code-deposit costs. Flash Loan Proxy separates the execution program from the implementation responsible for interpreting it. Instead of deploying a new contract for each program, callers provide the program as calldata. The proxy temporarily caches the program and forwards it to an implementation that interprets and executes it. This design provides several benefits: Dynamic execution programs: Different programs can be supplied for different execution sessions without deploying a new contract. Callback coordination: The proxy can dispatch reentrant invocations to
events.title: ERC-8486: Flash Loan Proxy

Abstract Deploying and distributing private smart contracts, confidential L2/Validium state diffs, or permissioned intent payloads across Ethereum’s public P2P and Data Availability (DA) layers currently faces a fundamental metadata bottleneck. Even when contract bytecode or state is symmetrically encrypted, existing Broadcast Encryption (BE) and Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE) schemes require attaching an explicit cleartext header specifying either the authorized recipient indices, covering subsets, or the target access tree. In this post, we propose an architectural framework based on Stealth Attribute-Based Broadcast Encryption (Stealth ABBE) over BLS12-381 ( Zenodo Preprint ) for zero-metadata delivery of private contracts and encrypted state on Ethereum. By reformulating broadcast access control as a homomorphic blind Reed–Solomon decoding problem over 𝔽 256 using carry-free Base-3 packing in exponential ElGamal ciphertexts (𝔾 1 × 𝔾 1 ), Stealth ABBE achieves: O(1) Broadcast KEM Size (24.1 KiB amortized): Fits comfortably inside a single EIP-4844 blob (~19% of one 128 KiB blob) regardless of the total participant count N . Zero Visible Headers or Revocation Lists (0 Bytes): Access policies, cohort rosters, and revocation states are algebraically absorbed into the non-systematic Reed–Solomon codeword. events.excerpt: Hello, I’ve opened a PR for a new opcode, SLOTDURATION . It pushes the duration of the current slot, in milliseconds, onto the stack. PR: Add EIP: SLOTDURATION Opcode by Amxx · Pull Request #12619 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub Open questions: Current duration or historical lookup? The draft returns the current duration. The Rationale describes an alternative where the opcode takes a slot number and returns the duration in effect at that slot, or 0 for future slots. That would let contracts like Lido’s compute correct timestamps across duration changes. The cost is that the execution layer would have to keep the duration schedule. Which is more useful? Milliseconds. I chose ms to match SLOT_DURATION_MS and to support L2s with 100–250 ms block times. Any objections? 0 for “no regular interval.” Is this the right sentinel for on-demand chains, and should L1 execution clients still reject 0 ? Execution-layer decoupling. EIP-8198 deliberately keeps the execution layer unaware of the slot duration. The draft keeps the EL config-free, but it does add a header field. Is that acceptable to the EIP-8198 authors and to client teams? 3 posts - 3 participants Read full topic
events.title: EIP-8484: SLOTDURATION Opcode

events.excerpt: Hello, This topic is intended to be complementary to the Kusama set reduction discussion in Proposal discussion: Adapting Kusama to demand and its JAM future - #10 by Lederstrumpf . My intent is that the discussion there remains focused on strategy, and this one on methodology. But since flaws in / potential improvements to methodology inform strategy, I welcome critical feedback on the findings of the following two reports: The decentralization report: hambro.ch/kusama/set-reductions/decentralization/ The coretime report: hambro.ch/kusama/set-reductions/coretime/ I suggest reading the strategy post on the reduction thread first to grok the intent, before delving into the reports - they’re already fairly verbose just from data explainers, so I’ve not stitched them into a flowing bedtime essay. Decentralization report The goal of the decentralization report is to identify how decentralization metrics changed with the last/first reduction ( section A ), to gauge how further reductions would impact decentralization ( section B ). Two key decisions this begs for: How do we define decentralization? How do we reliably identify validator clusters - a lot of these stashes lacking onchain identity - that share the same operator massaging them? For the decentralization question, I broadly ascribe to a combination of “number of operators I have to whack with a wrench or bribe with cash$ to break BFT” (Nakamoto coefficient, see A2 ), and “power distribution from smallest to largest operators by seat count” (Gini coefficient, see B5 , and distribution of operator size classes, see A4 ,

events.excerpt: Discussion topic for EIP-8477: Recent Block Bound Delegation Authorizations . Motivated by the recent EIP-7702 sweeps that happened on Binance 16 this proposal in essence prevents long term storage of EIP-7702 signatures for later playback. This proposal limits the delayed use of unused EIP-7702 authorizations. Each authorization signs a recent execution block number and its block header hash, in addition to the existing chain ID, delegation address, and nonce. For inclusion in execution block N , the signed block must be one of its preceding 256 ancestors and its hash must match that ancestor. An anchor exactly 256 blocks behind remains eligible; one 257 blocks behind is ineligible. The current block and future blocks are excluded. Freshness is checked during native authorization processing, before signature recovery or authority-specific state access. An expired or mismatched anchor skips that authorization using EIP-7702’s existing skip-on-failure behavior. It does not consume the authority’s nonce through that entry or clear an existing delegation. Structurally malformed authorizations invalidate the transaction. The draft applies the same freshness requirement to installation, replacement, and zero-address revocation. Installed delegations remain in effect after their authorization’s anchor expires. The proposal limits the inclusion window of an unused signature; it does not expire installed delegation or prevent an attacker with live signing access from promptly using a fresh signature.
